final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Christian Dior reshaped fashion by reimagining what already existed. Each season, Dior's ateliers invite clients to bring a treasured piece from any year: a tired Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior, an inherited coat. The petites mains re-cut, repair and reinterpret it into the season's silhouette. A selection appears in a runway moment and a film series beside the new collection, each with its owner and memory. Selection criteria are published and open to clients worldwide. A permanent atelier repair and alteration service keeps the idea running year-round, and a seasonal ledger shows pieces kept in use, atelier hours and materials reused. Reuse becomes a creative act, and Dior shows it is always becoming.
follow_up_questions: How could the selection process itself become part of the story, so that being chosen, and not being chosen, still deepens a client's bond with the house?
What would the standing, everyday version of this idea look like for a client whose piece never reaches the runway, and how could it feel as special as the seasonal event?
How might the creative director's own design language meet the owner's memory, so that each transformation is a true collaboration and not just a restoration?

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside every well-made Dior garment is a hidden inch: spare fabric in the seams, called a seam allowance, that lets the piece be taken in or let out over decades. People can book a refit, adjust a favourite piece, or pass it on, each framed as 'the next inch' of its story. For leather and shoes, resoling, re-edging and re-strapping play the same role. final_proposal.idea: Every first paycheck was payment for something you made: the shop flyer, the chalkboard menu, the rota, the slide the boss needed by Friday. required_elements.element: The 'Together' gift: a small virtual Mastercard gift (a coffee, haircut or bowl of noodles) that only activates when sender and receiver are both present
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes the payment the invitation. The sender doesn't have to admit loneliness, and the receiver gets a specific, low-pressure reason to say yes.

required_elements.element: A simple presence handshake (QR or tap-to-confirm at the venue) instead of complex geolocation
required_elements.what_it_does: Verifies that two people are together reliably and cheaply, which makes a pilot feasible. It also avoids continuous location tracking, which protects trust.

required_elements.element: Open Tap: gifts distributed through befriending charities, neighbourhood groups and new-parent circles
required_elements.what_it_does: Reaches people outside existing social circles, who are the people most affected by loneliness, so the idea doesn't only serve those who already have someone to invite.

required_elements.element: Safe, partner-led design for Open Tap (vetted partners, group-first or hosted meet-ups, opt-in matching)
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes meetings between people who don't know each other safe and comfortable, so Open Tap is credible and responsible.

required_elements.element: Local independent venues as the only places the gift can be used
required_elements.what_it_does: Puts meetings in real third places, keeps the money in the neighbourhood and makes the experience feel local, not corporate.

required_elements.element: Small gift values and unbranded venue experiences
required_elements.what_it_does: Keeps the idea from seeming gimmicky or like a commercialisation of loneliness, so the gesture stays about the meeting and not the money.

required_elements.element: Neutral framing: a gift for any reason, never labelled 'for lonely people'
required_elements.what_it_does: Removes stigma so people can send and accept the gift without feeling pitied or exposed.

required_elements.element: Success measured by meetings made and repeat meetings, not spend
required_elements.what_it_does: Shows the idea achieves its purpose, builds credibility and avoids looking like a spending-driven stunt.

focus_check.development_plan: Make the idea more feasible by launching a technically simple first version (tap or QR handshake, capped gift values, a handful of independent venues) in one city. Make it more inclusive by treating Open Tap as a co-equal pillar designed with charity partners from the start. Make it more human by giving the venue a defined welcome role and by framing the gift as an everyday gesture. Make it more credible by setting a clear privacy principle and measuring meetings made, repeat meetings and partner-reported connection.

borrowed_elements.element: Venue welcome layer: staff trained for gentle, warm greeting and a 'regulars'-style table or counter for Together gifts
borrowed_elements.why_needed: The gift gets two people through the door, but the venue shapes whether the meeting feels comfortable and leads to a second one. It also gives Open Tap guests a welcoming place to arrive.

revisions_after_selection.change: Replaced two-phone geolocation proximity checks with a simple tap or QR confirmation handshake for the first version.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces technical risk and makes a small pilot feasible. It also avoids location-tracking concerns that could damage trust in a financial brand.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made Open Tap a co-equal launch pillar, designed with charity and community partners from day one, rather than an add-on to the peer-to-peer gift.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Without it the idea mainly serves people who already have someone to invite, so it would miss the most isolated.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added safeguards for Open Tap: vetted partners, hosted or group-first meet-ups and opt-in participation.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Meetings between people who don't know each other need to be safe and comfortable, and partners need to be able to run the pilots responsibly.

revisions_after_selection.change: Capped gift values at a small everyday amount and required unbranded venue experiences.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents the idea from reading as a gimmick or as brand commercialisation of loneliness.

revisions_after_selection.change: Framed the gift as a gesture for any reason, with no mention of loneliness in the sender's or receiver's experience.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Removes the stigma of being seen as lonely or pitied, which would otherwise reinforce the barrier the idea is meant to remove.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed the venue welcome layer from C4: light staff training and a Together table or counter.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Turns the venue into an active part of making the meeting comfortable and repeatable, which strengthens the link to independent third places.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a clear privacy principle: no inference of loneliness from spending data and no use of the C1 mapping approach.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects trust in Mastercard and keeps the idea about an offer people choose to accept, not surveillance.

revisions_after_selection.change: Expanded measurement to meetings made, repeat meetings and partner-reported connection, not only spend.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A single meeting doesn't prove loneliness is eased. Repeat contact is a more credible signal and gives partners and press a more meaningful result.

final_proposal.title: Pay Together
final_proposal.idea: Pay Together is a small gift of money that only works when two people are in the same place. Send a friend, neighbour or old colleague a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles through a virtual Mastercard. It unlocks only when both of you tap in at the same independent venue. The payment is the invitation, so nobody has to say 'I'm lonely, shall we meet?' For people with no one to send it to, Open Tap hands the same gift to befriending charities, new-parent circles and neighbourhood groups, who use it to host real meet-ups. Gifts stay small, venues stay unbranded and staff are trained to welcome people warmly. The first pilot runs in one city with a handful of venues and charity partners, and success is counted in meetings made, not money spent.
follow_up_questions: Which life moments (moving city, a new baby, retirement, bereavement, a first week at work) are the most natural entry points, where an invitation is wanted but hard to give, and who is the most trusted person to send it?
How could the gift be designed so that receiving it feels like being valued and not like charity or pity, in its wording, its look and the way it arrives?
What would make two people keep meeting after the gift is spent, and how could the campaign hand the habit over to venues and communities so it doesn't depend on Mastercard's money?

final_proposal.idea: Once a year, Dior hangs a sign on its Paris flagship: Fermé pour réparations. For one day, nothing new is sold, in store or online. element_review.selected_core_idea: Mastercard admits that the fastest payment in history quietly deleted the last small human exchange at the till, and gives anyone a way to opt back in: pause the tap, and the merchant answers with an unhurried sound, a counter signal and a minute of conversation.

candidate_elements.element: Merchant and community onboarding for people who are hesitant about digital payments, with staff trained to offer patient, unhurried help at the till
candidate_elements.purpose: Extends the 'minute of time' to people who avoid tapping out of fear or low confidence. It adds a trust and inclusion layer that fits Mastercard's credentials and reaches some of the most isolated people.
candidate_elements.reason: It folds into the same mechanic without a separate programme: the unhurried signal also means 'happy to help you pay.' It broadens the audience beyond the already comfortable and makes the idea more credible. It is a light add-on, not a volunteer scheme, so it avoids the CSR and pilot-only problems.

candidate_elements.element: Volunteer pairing of young people with older adults on shopping trips
candidate_elements.purpose: Creates emotional intergenerational stories.
candidate_elements.reason: It needs a separate programme, is hard to scale, and risks sounding patronising. It would replace the simple opt-in mechanic with a managed service.

candidate_elements.element: A 'coffee's on me' credit that is redeemed only when two people meet
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives people a low-pressure excuse to reconnect with someone they have drifted from.
candidate_elements.reason: It depends on bank and app partners, enters a crowded P2P space, and serves people who already have contacts. It would slow the launch and pull the idea away from the till.

candidate_elements.element: Open-seat table markers and Mastercard-funded first rounds for strangers
candidate_elements.purpose: Turns a venue into an invitation to company.
candidate_elements.reason: It asks lonely people to take a large social leap and raises safety and consent concerns. It undermines the non-stigmatising, anyone-can-join quality that makes C1 strong.

candidate_elements.element: A time-limited 'Slow Hour' pilot with a founding group of independent merchants in a few neighbourhoods, using quiet-hour windows
candidate_elements.purpose: Secures real merchant participation before launch and prevents queue pressure, directly answering the two main concerns.
candidate_elements.reason: It makes the idea credible and operable from day one. A committed founding set avoids a gimmick that fails at the till, and quiet hours make the opt-in workable.

candidate_elements.element: A candid brand admission in the launch, acknowledging that speed has a cost, backed by a plain commitment that the slow option never becomes a fee or a charge
candidate_elements.purpose: Answers 'isn't Mastercard the reason things got faster?' by owning it, and protects the idea from looking opportunistic.
candidate_elements.reason: The candour is what makes the idea believable. Stating that slowness is free and never monetised keeps the intent clear and the tone honest.

candidate_elements.element: A customer-side 'pause' gesture that shopkeepers learn to recognise, such as a deliberate hover of the card before the tap
candidate_elements.purpose: Lets customers signal that they have a minute without speaking, so no one has to self-identify as lonely.
candidate_elements.reason: It is part of making the opt-in mechanic work and keeps it silent, simple and shareable. It supports the core idea rather than adding a new one.

revisions_after_selection.change: Launch as a founding 'Slow Hour' pilot with committed independent merchants (cafes, markets, corner shops) in a few neighbourhoods, in quiet-hour windows, before wider rollout.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Addresses the risk of a gimmick if merchants do not participate and the queue and busy-shop limits, by making participation real and the setting suitable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a silent customer gesture (the card-hover pause) that merchants are briefed to recognise and answer with the unhurried sound and counter signal.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Makes opting in effortless and non-stigmatising, so no one has to say they are lonely or ask for time.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded in a light version of C2's inclusion angle: the unhurried signal also means staff will patiently help anyone unsure about paying digitally.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reaches people who are most cut off, and strengthens Mastercard's trust and inclusion credentials, without a separate CSR programme.

revisions_after_selection.change: Built the launch around an open admission that speed has had a cost, with a clear promise that the slow option is always free.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Turns the 'Mastercard made things faster' objection into the source of credibility and prevents the idea from being read as a commercial play.

final_proposal.title: Take Your Time
final_proposal.idea: Tap-to-pay made paying faster, and quietly removed the last small conversation in many people's day. Mastercard says so openly, and offers a way back. Founding independent shops, cafes and markets display a counter signal and use a slower, unhurried version of Mastercard's payment sound. A customer who hovers their card for a beat is saying 'I've got a minute,' and the merchant answers with a chat, or patient help for anyone unsure about paying digitally. Nobody has to say they are lonely. It starts in quiet hours in a few neighbourhoods, is always free, and gives Priceless its smallest and most universal moment: a minute of someone's time.
follow_up_questions: What would the unhurried sound feel like, and how might it become as recognisable as the original tap sound without annoying merchants or other customers?
Which kinds of merchants and neighbourhoods hold the most unnoticed daily loneliness, and what would make their owners want to take part rather than feel obliged?
How could the campaign show real, unscripted minutes at the till without turning customers' private moments into content?

focus_check.core_direction: Turn the first paycheck into a creative milestone by inviting people to publish a 'First Paid' receipt that pairs the work they made to earn their first money with the date and who paid them, building a public gallery of the work that started careers.

required_elements.what_it_does: Gives people a simple, ownable, repeatable format that makes the insight (we remember the work, not the number) visible and shareable.

candidate_elements.reason: It supports the core idea and strengthens the status flip: a Cannage Darn becomes proof of a piece's biography. candidate_elements.element: Future-pattern card showing how a piece could be altered or repaired for another decade of wear
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes longevity tangible at the point of care or sale.
candidate_elements.reason: It belongs to a designed-for-reuse capsule. In this idea the dated mend card already does the job of making longevity tangible, and a second card would dilute it.

candidate_elements.element: Capsule of new pieces designed with mend-ready zones or seam allowances
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds a product-side proof point that repair is part of design.
candidate_elements.reason: It depends on the creative studio's calendar and risks reading as utilitarian. It is better as a later chapter once the Cannage Darn has cultural traction.

candidate_elements.element: Pop-up repair salons in major cities as the launch moment

candidate_elements.element: Runway debut: the Cannage Darn appears on the house's own new collection looks, on pieces the studio has deliberately mended
candidate_elements.purpose: Shows the signature has fashion authority and is not a service add-on, which answers the risk of a utilitarian or sustainability-led reading.
candidate_elements.reason: It places the mend inside Dior's fantasy and craft world and gives the press a fashion story. It also guards against the visible-mending cliché by making the mend a Dior design code. It uses assets the house already controls.

candidate_elements.element: Mend-turnaround promise and phased rollout (by boutique and by heritage piece such as Bar jacket and Lady Dior first)
candidate_elements.purpose: Protects atelier capacity and keeps the service credible if demand spikes.
candidate_elements.reason: Bottlenecks are the main operational risk. Phasing and clear expectations keep the promise believable and create a sense of scarcity that suits the house.

candidate_elements.element: Care-first framing: the campaign celebrates long ownership and careful wear, with the mend as the reward for keeping a piece, not as an invitation to damage it
candidate_elements.purpose: Neutralises the risk of seeming to celebrate damage or discourage careful ownership.
candidate_elements.reason: It refines the tone of the existing idea and makes sure that the visible mend reads as a mark of devotion, not carelessness.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light provenance function to the dated mend card, so the card travels with the piece and records later owners and mends.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It strengthens the status flip by making a mend part of a piece's story and value, and it takes the useful part of C1 without the resale operation.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a short run of Dior-only repair salons in a few cities as the launch moment, and not a permanent network.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The campaign needs a public, press-friendly debut that lets people see the petites mains work. Limiting it to Dior pieces keeps capacity manageable and the meaning Dior-specific.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a runway and collection debut in which the studio uses the Cannage Darn as a design code on new looks.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives the signature fashion authority and keeps the idea from being read as a customer-service gesture or a utilitarian turn.

revisions_after_selection.reason: It manages the capacity bottleneck, ties repair to heritage, and keeps the choice open for owners who do not want a visible mend.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the tone as a reward for careful, long ownership, where the mend marks devotion and not damage.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It reduces the risk that the campaign appears to celebrate damage or discourage careful ownership.

final_proposal.title: The Cannage Darn
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into a signature. The ateliers develop a hand-stitched mend based on the cannage lattice, which owners can choose to leave visible, as a mark of a well-loved piece, or have made invisible. Each mended piece returns with a dated card recording why its owner kept it, and the card travels with the piece if it is passed on. The mend debuts on the runway as a Dior code, then arrives in a short run of Dior-only repair salons, starting with the Bar jacket and the Lady Dior. The campaign celebrates the most-worn pieces and shows that the best Dior is the one you never stopped wearing.

How could the house manage demand and exclusivity so the mend feels like an earned honour and the atelier is never overwhelmed?

final_proposal.title: Take Your Time
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying the fastest it has ever been, and admits that it also quietly removed the last small conversation of many people's day. So it gives a minute back. How could the idea spread beyond physical tills, for example to self-checkouts, online orders or delivery handovers, without losing its human warmth?

final_proposal.title: Lucky Thread
final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into hems for luck. Now, every Dior piece that returns to the atelier for repair or restyling is finished with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining. It can't be bought, only earned by keeping a piece alive, and the artisan who mended it is credited by name. Wear becomes a badge, and repair becomes a ritual of the house. It launches with live stitching at 30 Montaigne, appears on the runway on clients' own marked pieces, and rolls out from iconic lines outward. A light repair record makes each mark verifiable in resale. If a piece can't be saved, the atelier offers a reinterpretation or an archival keepsake. The mark is never sold or licensed.

How could the mending artisan become a recognised figure of the house, and what would it mean for them to sign their work?
If the muguet is only earned, what other moments of devotion to a Dior piece (inheriting, passing on, wearing for decades) could the house recognise in the same way?

final_proposal.title: The Mark of Time: Dior's Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: Dior invites owners to treat a repair as a second signature. When a Bar jacket, Saddle bag or Lady Dior returns to the atelier, the client chooses: an invisible mend, or a visible one stitched by hand in Dior's own thread, finished with a small atelier mark and the name of the craftsperson who made it. The wear stays; only what is needed is mended. Campaign imagery treats creases, patina and stitches with the reverence of a runway look, featuring real owners and their pieces. The inversion: a mended Dior can mean more than a pristine one, because it carries the maison's hand and a life lived. It launches with a capsule of iconic pieces and a waiting list, keeping it exclusive and within atelier capacity, and giving owners a reason to repair with Dior and nowhere else.
follow_up_questions: What should the second signature look like, so that it is instantly recognisable as Dior yet subtle enough that an owner would be proud to show it?
Which real owners and which pieces would make people feel that a mend adds value, and how could they be found and shown without turning their stories into advertising?
How could the waiting list and the mark itself become objects of desire, for example through rarity, ceremony or collectability, without making repair feel like a luxury only a few can reach?

Your insights are revealing. Your ideas are platformable. Your wild ideas are provocative but strategically grounded. You don't write slogans -- you ignite campaigns.

reasoning.note: thinking tokens are not reported separately; output_tokens_total includes them

writing_notes.intended_reader: The reader is a Canva marketing or brand lead, or a client-side decision maker, who knows Canva's products and B2B positioning well but has not seen the four candidate directions in detail. They want a clear, usable campaign idea they can react to, not a strategy deck.

reader_needs.point: The core insight: the first paycheck is confusing and badly designed, and that confusion is a shared, slightly funny experience.
reader_needs.why: Everything else in the idea rests on this truth, so the reader must feel it before they judge the campaign.

reader_needs.point: What Canva actually does: it redesigns the pay stub experience and provides free templates, using fictional sample data only.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs a concrete, tangible action so they can picture the campaign and see the product in use.

reader_needs.point: Who benefits: first-time earners get clarity and employers or HR teams get a ready-to-use tool.
reader_needs.why: This shows why the idea fits Canva's B2B and productivity positioning and does not read as a consumer-only stunt.

reader_needs.point: How it stretches: the platform 'Design is how things make sense' can run across several formats, with guardrails against advice and data risks.
reader_needs.why: The reader must judge whether this is a campaign platform and whether it is safe to run.

terms_to_explain.explanation: The surprise of seeing that the amount you earned before deductions is much larger than the amount that lands in your bank account.
The document that comes with a paycheck and itemises pay, taxes and deductions. It is also called a payslip.
A before-and-after content format in which a real, confusing pay stub layout is shown next to a clear redesigned version.

tone_choices.choice: Warm and lightly humorous, centred on the 'where did my money go?' feeling.
tone_choices.reason: The truth is relatable and a little funny, and humour keeps the idea from feeling dry or like a finance lecture.

tone_choices.choice: Plain, short sentences with no jargon.
tone_choices.reason: The proposal should demonstrate the clarity it promises, so it should be easy for any reader to follow.

tone_choices.choice: Confident about the idea but explicit about its limits (explanation, not advice).
tone_choices.reason: Naming the guardrails builds trust with the reader and shows the risks have been thought through.

outline: The human truth: the first paycheck arrives and nobody understands it.
The idea in one line: Canva redesigns the pay stub experience.
What people get: a visual makeover and free templates.
Who it serves: first-time earners and the employers or HR teams who hand them the stub.
How it runs: makeover reveals, creator explainers, employer toolkits and OOH.
Guardrails: fictional data and explanation only, with disclaimers.

clarity_checks.check: Word limit
clarity_checks.how: Count the words in the idea text and cut until it is at or under 150.

clarity_checks.check: Jargon scan
clarity_checks.how: Check every term against the explained list and replace or define anything an outsider might not know.

clarity_checks.check: Emotional centre
clarity_checks.how: Confirm the first-paycheck feeling appears in the opening and the proposal is not just a template pitch.

clarity_checks.check: Open questions quality
clarity_checks.how: Make sure each of the three questions is open-ended, distinct from the others and usable for generating new ideas.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an explicit 'first-paycheck moment' anchor: the campaign launches around real firsts, such as first-job season and graduation, with stories from first-time earners in retail, food service and labor as well as office work.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps the emotional core at the centre and addresses the risk that the idea feels dry or only about documents.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded the best parts of C1 into the employer toolkit: a 'Welcome to Payday' template pack with a personal note, a visual explainer and a team shout-out.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps the new hire's experience central while giving managers a practical way to take part, and it strengthens the B2B angle.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed the tone of C4's 'now it's official' feeling for the creative voice, without building the identity kit.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It adds emotional warmth and the sense of proof of adulthood without overlapping with familiar Canva resume use cases.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set guardrails as part of the idea: fictional sample data only, templates that explain categories in general terms, no personalised tax guidance, and a clear disclaimer.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This manages the tax-advice and payroll-data sensitivity concerns from the start.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the makeover as a template that employers can adapt to the layout of their own payroll information, not as a replacement for official payroll documents.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the idea practical and avoids implying Canva produces legal pay documents.

final_proposal.title: The Paycheck, Explained
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is a small miracle, and a total mystery. You worked hard, and then a dense document shows a much smaller number than you expected. Canva redesigns that moment. We publicly give the pay stub a makeover, turning the gross-to-net shock into a clear, friendly visual story, and release free templates that employers, HR teams and small business owners can use to explain pay in plain, visual language, with a welcome note and team shout-out built in. It runs as makeover reveals, creator explainers, employer toolkits and OOH that mimics ugly pay stubs. Everything uses fictional data and explains rather than advises. The platform: design is how things make sense.
follow_up_questions: Which first-paycheck stories, such as a first retail shift, a summer job or a side hustle, would make people feel most seen, and who should tell them?
What other confusing documents in early adult life (a lease, a benefits form, a bill) could Canva make clear next, and which would have the most emotional pull?
How could employers and HR teams take part in a way that feels sincere to the new hire rather than corporate?

final_proposal.idea: Most lonely people aren't short of friends to call. They're stuck on the awkward first step and the guilt of leaving it too long. revisions_after_selection.change: Made Slow Tap and the sonic signature optional second-phase layers, not part of the launch.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a commitment to publish pilot results and keep a standing programme.

final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying faster. Now it admits that not everything should be. candidate_elements.reason: The brief's risk list names cashier labour directly, and the selection depends on cashiers wanting to take part. Without it the idea could exploit workers and fail. It supports the core idea and does not change it.

candidate_elements.element: Recognition for merchants and staff who know customers by name and order (a light 'known here' nod on the Slow Lane sign or in the programme)
candidate_elements.purpose: Brings in the warmth of 'being a regular' and gives merchants a positive way to be recognised, without building a separate loyalty-style scheme.

candidate_elements.element: Full 'Regulars' mark and city-wide rally to protect neighbourhood businesses, using aggregate anonymised data
candidate_elements.purpose: Would add a small-business agenda and a data-led story about belonging.

candidate_elements.element: Refundable deposit mechanism ('Priceless Plans') to turn plans into meetings
candidate_elements.purpose: Would add a behavioural commitment device with a product-like feature.
candidate_elements.reason: It monetises friendship, needs new products and regulatory work that would delay launch, and speaks to people who already have plans. It does not suit a no-stigma, everyone-welcome checkout idea.

candidate_elements.element: Pre-paid seat or meal that a stranger can claim
candidate_elements.purpose: Would add a generosity mechanic and a photogenic visual.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a familiar pay-it-forward model, raises stranger-matching and pity issues, and would add a second, different mechanic that weakens the clarity of the Slow Lane.

candidate_elements.purpose: Answers merchant throughput worries and the risk of being dismissed as a stunt by giving a clear business case and a sustained commitment.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief's main concerns are contradiction with speed, merchant resistance and the gimmick risk. A transparent pilot with published results answers all three and does not change the core idea.

candidate_elements.purpose: Adds authority on loneliness, helps measure impact and protects against a brand claiming a social issue it has no expertise in.

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying faster. Now it admits that not everything should be. In partner grocers and pharmacies, one checkout lane is marked 'This lane takes its time'. Cashiers who choose to host it are given paid time and recognition to chat. Anyone can use it, whether they want conversation, are in no rush, or just like the pace, so nobody has to say they're lonely. A 'Slow Tap' terminal mode swaps the efficient beep for a warmer pause. It starts as a measured pilot at off-peak hours, with a loneliness research partner and published results, including the throughput cost. If it works, it grows into Slow Hour and Slow Day. The checkout, often the only conversation someone has all day, becomes the place where Priceless happens.

What evidence would convince a sceptical merchant that a slower lane is worth the throughput cost: a rise in basket size, repeat visits, staff retention, or something else?

candidate_elements.element: A permanent, scalable atelier repair and alteration service that runs year-round, with the seasonal event as its showcase
candidate_elements.purpose: Counters the 'one-off stunt' and elitism concerns by giving every client a standing route for care, while the seasonal event stays the creative, scarce moment.
candidate_elements.reason: The selection reasoning already relies on it to manage capacity and credibility. Without it, the idea reaches only a handful of clients and looks like a stunt. It should be stated explicitly in the proposal.

candidate_elements.element: A transparent, regionally open selection process, with pieces chosen by story and condition as well as by prestige of the item, and a published impact report each season (pieces kept in use, atelier hours, materials reused)
candidate_elements.purpose: Guards against accusations of elitism and greenwashing and makes scarcity feel fair and credible.
candidate_elements.reason: The two biggest risks of C2 are access and credibility. Open criteria and specific, verifiable figures answer both, and they are consistent with a luxury house that values rigour.

candidate_elements.element: A 'second chapter' discount or trade-in voucher for clients who bring in a piece
candidate_elements.purpose: Would encourage participation and drive store traffic.
candidate_elements.reason: Incentives of this kind move the idea towards discounting and undermine pricing power, which the idea is meant to protect. The reward should be the atelier's attention, not a price cut.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a permanent year-round atelier repair and alteration service as the base of the platform, with the seasonal transformation event as its creative showcase.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Capacity limits and the one-off-stunt reading are the main risks. A standing service makes the commitment real and open to all clients.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a lineage note for each transformed piece, with the owner's story and the atelier's work, which stays with the piece.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It brings C1's provenance value into C2 at low cost and strengthens the emotional storytelling, without building a resale system.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a discreet embroidered star inside each transformed piece as a signature.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives the platform an ownable, shareable mark with roots in Dior's heritage, and avoids the visible-repair and fake-distress problems of C3.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added transparent selection criteria open to clients across regions and eras, and a published impact report each season.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It addresses the elitism and greenwashing concerns with specific, verifiable commitments.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior reshaped what already existed. Now every season, the ateliers do it for clients. Anyone can bring in a treasured piece from any year, such as a tired Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior or an inherited coat. The petites mains re-cut, repair and reinterpret a selection into the season's silhouette. The results appear on the runway and in a film series told through their owners' memories. Each carries a small embroidered star inside and a lineage note that stays with it. Selection is transparent and open across regions. A year-round repair and alteration service keeps the promise going between shows, and each season Dior publishes what it kept in use: pieces, atelier hours and materials. Reuse becomes the most creative thing a house can do.

How should the transformed pieces appear on the runway so the audience feels the owner's story and not only the new silhouette?
What impact measures could Dior publish each season that are specific and verifiable and still sound like Dior, not like a sustainability report?

Your insights are revealing. Your ideas are platformable. Your wild ideas are provocative but strategically grounded. You don't write slogans -- you ignite campaigns.

focus_check.core_purpose: To address the gap between the excitement of a first paycheck and the confusion of deductions and an unreadable payslip, for first-time earners and the employers and HR teams who want to onboard them well, while giving Canva a credible role in B2B and productivity workflows.
focus_check.core_direction: Canva redesigns the first payslip so it explains itself in plain, visual language and doubles as a keepsake, delivered through employer and payroll templates and a privacy-safe restyle option for individuals.

required_elements.element: A plain-language visual payslip template that explains what each line is (gross, tax, social contributions, pension, net) in descriptive, non-advisory terms
required_elements.what_it_does: Resolves deduction shock and proves 'design is clarity' in a single before-and-after image.

required_elements.element: Employer and HR adoption route through Canva for Teams, with brand-kit-ready templates and a small pilot with employers or payroll providers
required_elements.what_it_does: Gives the B2B buyer a concrete use case and a measurable commercial outcome (template use, Teams sign-ups).

required_elements.element: Redaction-first individual route: users rebuild their own payslip from scratch or from a blank template with numbers entered manually or masked, with nothing uploaded or stored by default
required_elements.what_it_does: Lets first-time earners benefit without partners and removes the privacy risk of handling real pay data.

required_elements.element: Descriptive-only content guardrails and a plain disclaimer, with explanation copy reviewed by a tax or payroll expert per market
required_elements.what_it_does: Keeps the idea on the safe side of financial guidance and makes it credible across countries.

required_elements.element: A hero before-and-after demonstration (real, anonymised payslips, redesigned) seeded through press, social and creators
required_elements.what_it_does: Turns the product into a cultural conversation and gives the idea visible, shareable proof.

required_elements.element: A shareable keepsake layer: a 'first payslip' card with the numbers hidden and a line of thanks to someone who helped
required_elements.what_it_does: Adds the emotional payoff that makes new earners want to share and brings new users in through recipients.

focus_check.development_plan: Sharpen the idea into a two-layer system: a 'Clear Payslip' template pack for employers (the B2B engine) and a 'My First Payslip' restyle tool for individuals (the cultural engine). Make it concrete with a defined launch: three or four markets, a pilot with a few employers or a payroll provider, and a hero before-and-after film and image series. Make it feasible by launching with templates that need no integration, setting content guardrails (describe, never advise) and keeping personal data out of Canva's systems by default. Define the platform logic ('Make the confusing clear') so later chapters can cover tax statements, benefits and pension letters.

borrowed_elements.element: Gratitude keepsake: a first-payslip card with the amount hidden and a thank-you to the person who helped, ready to send
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It gives the practical redesign an emotional, shareable ending, so the idea speaks to feeling as well as clarity. It also creates a natural route for sharing without exposing pay data.

borrowed_elements.element: Payslip explainer as part of a wider new-hire welcome
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It positions the payslip template as the entry point to broader onboarding use for HR teams, which strengthens the B2B case and gives employers a reason to adopt.

revisions_after_selection.change: Split the idea into two clear layers: an employer template pack and an individual 'My First Payslip' restyle tool.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Each audience needs a distinct entry point, and the individual route must work without payroll partners, which removes the main dependency risk.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the individual route redaction-first and manual: users enter or mask figures themselves, and nothing is uploaded or stored by default.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Handles the privacy concern directly and makes the campaign safe to launch and to talk about publicly.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added descriptive-only guardrails with expert review of explanation copy per market.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Payslip structures and terms differ by country, and explanations that drift into advice create reputational and regulatory risk.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a hero before-and-after demonstration built from anonymised, real payslips.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The idea's power lies in visible proof; without a seeded showcase it would sit as a template few people notice.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed the thank-you keepsake from C4 as an optional sharing layer.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Gives new earners an emotional reason to share and invites recipients into Canva, without moving the idea away from clarity.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed the welcome-kit logic from C1 as the next step for employers, not the launch product.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Shows HR buyers a path from one template to broader onboarding use while keeping the launch focused and distinctive.

final_proposal.title: The Payslip, Redesigned
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck should feel like a milestone, not a puzzle. Canva redesigns the first payslip so it explains itself: a visual, plain-language view of where the money went, describing each line without ever advising. Employers and payroll teams adopt it through Canva for Teams templates and brand kits, and new hires get a document they actually understand. Individuals can rebuild their own in Canva with figures typed in or masked, nothing stored, then turn it into a keepsake card with the numbers hidden and a thank-you to whoever helped them get there. The launch hero is a series of anonymised before-and-afters. The platform reads 'Make the confusing clear' and can grow to tax statements, benefits and pension letters.
follow_up_questions: Which other 'first-time' documents (a first lease, first tax return, first pension statement) cause the same mix of excitement and confusion, and could become the next chapter of the platform?
What would make an employer proud to show a redesigned payslip to candidates as part of its employer brand, and not just treat it as an HR admin fix?
How could the before-and-after be turned into something people want to post, so that clarity becomes a social flex and not only a service?

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the amount optional and hidden by default. People can show it, blur it, or swap it for 'hours it took' or a one-line memory.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Removes the privacy and comparison risk and keeps the focus on the work, which is the core insight.

revisions_after_selection.change: Widened 'First Paid' to cover any first work someone was trusted with: decks, flyers, résumés, posters, pitch materials, plus a 'first thing I made for someone' entry.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Not every first paycheck came from design. A broader definition keeps the platform inclusive without losing its focus on made things.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a pre-launch seeding phase with creators, Canva staff and well-known figures, each sharing a real first receipt before the gallery opens.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents an empty-room launch and shows the format's emotional tone to new contributors.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the payer as an optional 'thank-you tag' that lets the first client, boss or friend be credited and notified.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Makes sharing a gesture of gratitude rather than a disclosure, and adds a natural route to reach and earned attention.

revisions_after_selection.change: Moved the C1 team card and C3 invoice templates to supporting roles: a B2B 'first paid' moment for new hires and a template series for freelancers.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the strongest parts of the rejected ideas and connects the campaign to team adoption without diluting the single idea.

final_proposal.title: First Paid
final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. Canva turns that memory into a platform. People publish a 'First Paid' receipt that pairs the design that earned their first money with the date and an optional thank-you tag for whoever paid them. The amount is hidden unless they choose to share it. The definition of work is wide, from pitch decks to flyers to 'the first thing I made for someone'. Seeded with creators and Canva's own people, the gallery grows into a public record of careers beginning, and 'Made in Canva' becomes a badge of pride rather than a watermark.
follow_up_questions: What would make someone feel proud enough to post a first receipt, and what would make them hold back?
How could the gallery work for employers, such as a team 'First Paid' moment for new hires, without feeling like a corporate gimmick?
How should the format change across cultures where a first paycheck is a family event, a rite of passage, or rarely discussed?

Structure the rollout in three layers: seeded creators and small businesses as launch proof, open UGC through the template and OOH celebrating real first work, and a sustained B2B layer through employer and school onboarding. Add guardrails so the amount stays hidden and sensitive data is never requested.

borrowed_elements.element: The keepsake treatment: framing the first-pay moment as something worth honouring and displaying, rather than leaving in a drawer
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It gives the 'Paid for this' template a warm, collectible finish (a framed or scrapbook look) that supports sharing and emotional pull, while the work, not the payslip, remains the subject so privacy risk is avoided.

borrowed_elements.element: The shift into being a professional, with Brand Kit and document tools for the self-employed
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It gives freelancers and small-business owners a practical next step after sharing their first paid work, connecting the emotion to Canva's paid offer.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined 'work' broadly, so it includes non-visual first jobs through the story, such as a shift flyer, a handwritten menu or a rota.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Not every first job involves visual output or Canva. Widening the definition keeps the idea universal and answers the main concern.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the amount hidden by default a firm rule, replacing the figure with a feeling, a story or a 'what it taught me' line, and never asking for payslips.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Prevents comparison and pay-gap debate and avoids the privacy risk of sharing sensitive documents.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a keepsake-style template finish (framed or scrapbook look) borrowed from C2.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Adds emotional warmth and a reason to share, and makes the format feel collectible rather than like a generic hashtag.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a follow-on path for freelancers and small businesses to Brand Kit and Teams, borrowing the professional-identity idea from C1.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Links the emotional moment to Canva's B2B offer and gives the campaign a commercial outcome.

revisions_after_selection.change: Specified a three-layer rollout: seeded real stories, open UGC with OOH, and employer or school onboarding.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Strong seeding prevents the idea from feeling like a generic trend, and the onboarding layer extends its life beyond a single moment.

final_proposal.title: Paid For This
final_proposal.idea: A first paycheck is really a receipt for your first real piece of work. 'Paid for this' flips the usual payslip photo: people share the thing they made or did, whether a menu, pitch deck, logo, shift flyer or rota, with the amount hidden by default and a feeling in its place: 'Terrified. Proud. Rent covered.' A simple Canva template, with a framed, keepsake finish, makes it a one-minute post. Launch is seeded with real creators, small-business owners and young workers, and real first work appears in OOH. Employers, schools and Teams customers can use the same format to welcome new hires and celebrate their first paid work, with Brand Kit as the next step for freelancers turning pro. The paycheck becomes proof of ability, not salary.
follow_up_questions: Which first jobs and kinds of work would feel most surprising and moving to see celebrated, and how could the campaign find them beyond the usual creative scene?
How could employers and schools turn 'Paid for this' into a recurring onboarding ritual that makes Canva part of how teams welcome people to work?
What feelings, rather than figures, could become the campaign's recognisable language, and how might that language travel across markets and cultures?

Your thinking is strategic, surprising, and never cliché. You draw from human behaviour, cultural shifts, product truths, audience quirks, and category conventions -- wherever the best ideas live. Your insights are revealing. Your ideas are platformable. Your wild ideas are provocative but strategically grounded. You don't write slogans -- you ignite campaigns.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed 'Settle in person' from a replacement for payment into a deferred settlement. The money is held as an optional fallback, and if the meetup doesn't happen within a set window (for example 30 days), the original amount is sent automatically.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The main concern was that meetups may not happen. An automatic fallback protects the person who is owed, removes the awkwardness of chasing, and keeps the payments product trustworthy for a financial brand.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a gentle, mutual nudge mechanic: both people get a shared calendar prompt and a suggestion of a nearby partner cafe or restaurant, with no pressure messaging and no tracking of who cancels.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reduces friction between intent and action, which is where good intentions usually fail, while avoiding guilt or surveillance that would undercut the warmth of the idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the first phase as a limited pilot with one P2P partner and a small set of cafes in a single city, measuring only completed meetups, not personal data.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Addresses the gimmick risk by creating real usage proof, and keeps privacy exposure low and delivery realistic before scaling.

revisions_after_selection.change: Removed any loneliness language from the consumer-facing proposition. Loneliness appears only in the brand's purpose narrative and research partnerships, and the public hook stays 'Who do you owe one?'
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the idea stigma-free and widely relatable, so people take part because they owe a friend, not because they feel they have a problem.

final_proposal.title: Owe Me One
final_proposal.idea: When you split a bill or cover a friend's coffee, Mastercard adds a new option beside 'Pay back': 'Settle in person.' Instead of sending money, you set a shared date to meet. A payments brand choosing not to complete a transaction is the provocation: time with people is the one currency that can't be sent digitally. If the meetup doesn't happen within a set window, the payment goes through automatically, so no one is left out of pocket. It launches as a pilot with a P2P partner and local cafes, supported by the social question 'Who do you owe one?' It never labels anyone lonely. It simply turns small debts into reasons to show up.
follow_up_questions: What other small, everyday money moments could carry a built-in reason to see someone, and which of them is the most universal?
How could the campaign celebrate the meetups that actually happen, without turning friendship into a metric or a leaderboard?
If a payments brand can deliberately choose not to complete a transaction, what other things could it step back from to make room for people?

final_proposal.title: Tap Together
final_proposal.idea: Loneliness is hard to admit, but easy to cure with an invitation. Tap Together lets anyone send a prepaid 'on me' treat at a local business: a coffee, a haircut, a bowl of noodles. It only works when the sender's and receiver's cards tap at the same terminal in the same visit, so the gift can't be used alone. The sender takes the social risk; the receiver simply says yes. A warm invitation builder makes the first step easy, and a longer, softer sound marks the shared tap. Charity partners can send invitations for people with no one to ask. Piloted in a few cities with independent merchants, it drives footfall and counts shared visits.

If the shared visit repeated, what small ritual or reward would turn a one-off 'on me' into a regular habit of meeting up?

element_review.selected_core_idea: Dior reveals the hidden extra inch of seam allowance inside well-made couture as its quiet promise of a long life, and frames refitting, repair and passing a piece on as the 'next inch' of the garment's story.

candidate_elements.element: Real owners' emotional stories, told through the people who bring pieces back for a refit or hand them on
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds the emotional warmth that offsets the dryness of a technical detail. Gives the inch a human payoff and proof that the promise works in real lives.
candidate_elements.reason: The main concern for C2 is that the construction detail feels dry. Real owner stories fix this without the staged damage, the romanticised flaws or the creative-director dependency of the full C1 show.

candidate_elements.element: Couture show built on deliberately damaged garments (moth holes, torn hems) reinterpreted as signatures
candidate_elements.purpose: Creates a spectacle and press moment around imperfection.
candidate_elements.reason: It romanticises damage and could devalue expensive pieces. It also pulls the campaign toward a one-off event and away from the longevity promise, so it would compete with the core idea rather than support it.

candidate_elements.element: Atelier repairers shown performing refits, credited by first name, in close-up
candidate_elements.purpose: Shows who delivers the promise and makes the service tangible and credible. Adds craft intimacy and supports the capacity claim.
candidate_elements.reason: It serves as a storytelling layer inside C2 rather than a standalone idea. This avoids the 'craft hero' trope problem because the hands are always doing something specific: moving the inch for a real owner.

candidate_elements.element: Numbered provenance label and house-certified pre-owned programme
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives later owners a formal route into the story and covers reuse with a tangible offer.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a business-model decision with cannibalisation and privacy risks, and it would need heavy internal alignment. Keep it as a later extension. The core proposal covers reuse through re-gifting and refitting for a new owner, with no visible owner history.

candidate_elements.element: Refit for a new owner as a named service moment (the 'Next Inch' refit), available to first and later owners
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives later owners a way in without launching a full resale programme. Covers reuse and makes the behaviour clear: bring the piece in, have it re-fitted, wear it again.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief is repair and reuse. Without an explicit reuse action the idea leans too far toward first-owner repair. This is a light service layer that Dior can deliver with existing atelier capability.

candidate_elements.element: Published 'Inch Standard': a public commitment on seam allowance and repairability for core pieces, plus atelier capacity and turnaround commitments
candidate_elements.purpose: Backs the longevity claim with verifiable standards and protects against greenwashing accusations.
candidate_elements.reason: The biggest risk is an unbacked 'built to last' claim. A published, auditable standard turns the claim into a commitment and strengthens the product-truth advantage.

candidate_elements.element: Accessory equivalents of the inch (resoling, re-edging, re-strapping, re-lining) framed as 'the next inch'
candidate_elements.purpose: Stretches the metaphor to leather goods, shoes and accessories, where seam allowance matters less.
candidate_elements.reason: Dior's accessories are a large part of the business, and a garment-only idea would leave a gap. Treating the inch as a unit of extra life makes the metaphor portable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added real owners' stories (borrowed from C1) as the emotional engine, with no staged damage or runway spectacle.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This answers the concern that the technical detail may feel dry while avoiding the risk of romanticising damage.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made atelier hands (from C4) the way the inch is shown, with each refit credited by first name.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the promise tangible and credible, and it gives the story a human face without becoming a generic craft-hero film.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a named refit service open to first and later owners, with no previous-owner labelling or resale programme.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives people a clear action and covers reuse, while avoiding the cannibalisation, privacy and business-model risks of C3.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a published Inch Standard with atelier capacity and turnaround commitments.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It backs the longevity claim and reduces greenwashing risk.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined the inch as a unit of extra life, with accessory equivalents such as resoling, re-edging and re-strapping.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It stretches the metaphor beyond garments so the platform works across Dior's categories.

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside every well-made Dior couture piece, a hidden inch of seam allowance lets the garment be taken in, let out and re-fitted over decades. The campaign reveals that inch as Dior's quiet promise of a long life. Films follow real owners and atelier hands, credited by first name, as a piece is refitted for a changed body, a daughter or a new owner. The inch becomes a unit of extra life: a seam, a resoled heel, a re-edged bag. A published Inch Standard and a bookable Next Inch refit service turn the promise into a commitment and an action. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a single purchase.
follow_up_questions: What would a credible Inch Standard need to include, and which pieces, houses or price points could meet it today versus only in future collections?
How could the 'next inch' be made tangible for a new owner without exposing the previous owner's identity, for example through a ritual, object or moment at the refit?
Which non-garment equivalents of the inch (a heel, an edge, a strap, a lining) are the most surprising and visual, and how could each be filmed so the metaphor feels natural rather than stretched?

focus_check.core_purpose: Dior's brief is to make repair and reuse part of how people relate to luxury fashion. Today many Dior clients and aspirational buyers see repair as a fix for something broken, not as a luxury act, and the cure is to replace. The campaign addresses them.
focus_check.core_direction: Use the New Look's 80th anniversary to show that remaking what already exists is the highest form of couture. The ateliers transform owners' beloved garments, documented openly and revealed in a show where the original owners wear the results, backed by a repair and alteration service that anyone can use.

required_elements.element: Open call for a garment people cannot let go of, submitted with its story
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes the public the source of the content and ties reuse to memory and emotion instead of sustainability duty. This is what shifts the value of keeping a garment.

required_elements.element: Couture atelier remakes, documented from first cut to final fitting
required_elements.what_it_does: Shows that reuse gets the house's highest craft, so it reads as the pinnacle of luxury and not a concession. It also makes the effort and skill visible.

required_elements.element: Anniversary show finale with the original owners wearing the remade pieces
required_elements.what_it_does: Creates the hero moment and the ownable image. It gives the campaign a cultural peak and proves the pieces are worn, not just displayed.

required_elements.element: Broader repair and alteration service in boutiques, launched at the same moment as the couture remakes
required_elements.what_it_does: Turns the inspiration into a behaviour that many clients can adopt. It keeps the campaign credible and guards against greenwashing, because couture remakes are the showcase and the service is the offer.

required_elements.element: Public proof points on the service tier, such as pieces repaired and turnaround
required_elements.what_it_does: Backs the story with measurable commitment, so the campaign cannot be dismissed as a one-off anniversary gesture.

focus_check.development_plan: Make the idea more concrete and feasible by (1) phasing it: submissions open first, selection and early films follow, the show is the culmination, and the service tier continues afterwards; (2) pairing every couture remake with a launch of the everyday repair service so the two are announced as one idea; (3) defining eligibility, privacy and consent rules for owners; (4) setting up the documentary format as a serial, so the process builds anticipation before the show; (5) adding two light details from other candidates, an optional signature mark and a short provenance record, so remade and repaired pieces carry their story forward.

borrowed_elements.why_needed: Gives the transformation a recognisable, collectable signature and a visual cue that spreads on social media. It carries the idea beyond the show, and keeping it optional respects clients who prefer invisible mending.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. Dior invites people to submit the garment they can't let go of, with its story: a mother's coat, a wedding jacket, a worn-out favourite, from any label. The ateliers remake a selection into couture, filmed from first cut to final fitting. The anniversary show closes with the pieces worn by the people who gave them. Alongside, every Dior boutique launches a repair and alteration service, so remaking is the showcase and repair is open to all. Each remade piece carries an optional atelier mark and a record of its story. Reuse stops being a concession and becomes the highest form of luxury.

How could the campaign reach and move people who will never submit a garment or sit in the front row, without losing the intimacy of the stories?
What should Dior commit to publicly after the anniversary, so that in two years the idea is judged by lasting behaviour and not by one great show?

revisions_after_selection.change: Widened 'work' from visual output to anything a first pay was earned for. The story or feeling can sit beside a handwritten menu, a shift rota, a flyer for a shop opening or a first slide deck, and the format carries no requirement that the work be made in Canva.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Not every first job involved design. Without this, the idea would exclude many people and read as a product showcase. It keeps the universality of the first paycheck and lets Canva appear as one tool among the real work of work.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made 'amount hidden' a core rule of the format. The pairing is the work plus a feeling or a line, such as 'Paid for this. I was terrified. It was worth it.' Participants never show payslips or figures.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This removes the privacy risk of sharing payslips, reduces pay-gap comparison, and keeps the focus on pride rather than salary.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a seeding plan before launch: real first-work stories from creators, small-business owners, interns and first-time employees, shown through a creator series and OOH, then opened to the public through a template.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The biggest risk is a generic hashtag with no momentum. Seeding with real, specific stories sets the tone and quality of participation before the public joins.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a B2B extension: employers, schools and small-business teams get a 'First Paid For This' onboarding template that welcomes new starters by celebrating their first piece of work.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This ties the emotional idea to Canva's Teams and workplace offer, supports the productivity category, and gives the platform life beyond a seasonal social moment.

final_proposal.title: Paid For This
final_proposal.idea: A first paycheck is really a receipt for proof you can do something. Paid For This flips the familiar payslip photo and celebrates the work itself: the menu, pitch deck, flyer, logo, rota or social calendar that someone first got paid for. The amount is always hidden. Instead, people pair the work with a feeling or a one-line story. We seed it with real creators, interns and small-business owners through OOH and a creator series, then open it up with a simple Canva template anyone can use. A workplace version lets employers welcome new starters by celebrating their first piece of work. Pride replaces salary as the thing worth sharing.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job moments beyond design (a till shift, a tutoring session, a market stall) could carry the idea, and how would the format honour them without making Canva feel forced?
How could the 'hidden amount' become a creative device in its own right, such as a redaction bar, a sticker or a signature visual, so that it is recognisable at a glance and strengthens ownability?
Who are the right first voices to seed with, and what would make employers, schools or small-business networks want to adopt the onboarding version rather than just watch it?

reader_needs.point: Why it is distinctly Dior: it extends the couture fitting across a piece's whole life.
reader_needs.why: The idea only works if repair feels like couture, not maintenance, and that link is the reason it belongs to Dior.

reader_needs.point: What the repeatable mechanics are: the dated, signed label, named atelier hands, and real transformation stories.
reader_needs.why: These show the idea is a platform that can carry many chapters, not a one-off.

reader_needs.point: What must be true for it to work: atelier capacity, honest turnaround and pricing, a light check on secondhand pieces, and a tone that looks forward.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs to see that the main risks are known and can be managed before launch.

terms_to_explain.explanation: A return visit to the Dior atelier where a piece the owner already has is altered, recut or restored to suit who they are now.
The skilled artisans in Dior's ateliers who make and finish garments by hand, often unseen and unnamed.
Having worn or frayed edges of a bag, such as the leather trim, renewed so the piece looks cared for again.

tone_choices.choice: Confident and warm, with short, concrete sentences.
tone_choices.reason: It suits a luxury reader and keeps the idea easy to retell without sounding like marketing jargon.

tone_choices.choice: Lead with examples of transformation (a jacket let out, a coat recut for a daughter) before explaining the concept.
tone_choices.reason: Concrete images make the idea understood faster than abstract language, and they set the emotional register.

tone_choices.choice: Frame repair as an aspiration and a status act, and avoid the vocabulary of waste, guilt or sustainability.
tone_choices.reason: Luxury owners respond to desirability and craft, and guilt-led language would clash with the House's voice.

outline: Name the idea and say what it is in one sentence.
Give two or three vivid examples of a Second Fitting.
Explain the link to Dior's fitting and couture ritual.
Describe the mechanics: the signed, dated label and the named atelier hands.
Show how the story extends across film, boutique, client ledger and press.
State what must be true to deliver it, then end with the open questions.

clarity_checks.check: The idea can be repeated in one sentence.
clarity_checks.how: Read the first sentence alone and confirm it says who returns what to whom and for what purpose.

clarity_checks.check: Every Dior-specific term is understood by a non-specialist.
clarity_checks.how: Make sure petites mains, fitting and re-edged are used in a way that their meaning is clear from context.

clarity_checks.check: The proposal stays within 150 words.
clarity_checks.how: Count the words in the idea field and cut any sentence that does not help the reader understand or decide.

clarity_checks.check: Claims are grounded and not overpromised.
clarity_checks.how: Check that every benefit named ties to a mechanic in the idea and that capacity and turnaround are stated as conditions, not assumed.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light authentication step for secondhand pieces as a stated condition of the service.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The original idea welcomed secondhand owners but left open the brand-control and counterfeit risk, which would undermine exclusivity.

revisions_after_selection.change: Required that stories cover change and the present (a new job, a new body, a new city), not only inherited pieces.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The nostalgic, heirloom-only tone was flagged as a risk with younger audiences, and this keeps the platform feeling current.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the signed, dated label as the single recurring mark, with visible mending or embroidery as an optional finish only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps one clear ownable mechanic while still using the best part of C3 without making the campaign a trend.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made capacity, turnaround and pricing a launch condition, with the service starting in a limited number of ateliers and boutiques.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A broken promise would damage the idea more than anything else, so scale should follow what the atelier can deliver.

final_proposal.title: Second Fitting
final_proposal.idea: Dior was built on the first fitting: the moment a garment is made for one body. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be re-fitted for the life its owner is living now. A Bar jacket is let out, a mother's coat is recut for her daughter, a worn Lady Dior is re-edged. Each finished piece carries a dated, signed label naming the atelier hands who did the work. Real clients and their transformations drive films, boutique moments and press, with a new chapter for every stage of life. Keeping a Dior piece becomes the sign of taste. It starts small, with honest turnaround times and a light authenticity check for secondhand pieces.
follow_up_questions: Which life changes feel most current and surprising for younger audiences, and could a Second Fitting story be told about one of them without turning nostalgic?
How visible should the named petites mains become: credited on the label, present in boutiques, or the faces of the campaign, and what would they be comfortable with?
What would a Second Fitting need to cost, and how long could it take, before it stops feeling like a privilege and starts feeling like a service?

      "Highly visual and shareable, with immediate street-style and social potential",

      "Reads as design trend more than a deep behavior shift and may age quickly"
