element_review.selected_core_idea: Dior extends its founding ritual, the fitting, across the life of a piece: any Dior piece can return to the atelier to be re-fitted for the life its owner is living now, and it comes back with a dated, signed 'Second Fitting' label crediting the hands that did the work.

candidate_elements.element: Optional signature mend finish (a Dior motif such as a star, muguet or bee embroidered over a repair)
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives owners who want a visible mark a way to show the repair, adds a visual and shareable layer, and gives design teams a seasonal variation to work with.
candidate_elements.reason: It works as a client choice inside a Second Fitting, not as the idea itself. This avoids the kintsugi-trope and glamorized-damage concerns, because the mend is offered only when the owner wants it. It also gives younger audiences a more expressive way into the service.

candidate_elements.element: Living record of a piece's life (a client ledger of fittings, owners and transformations)
candidate_elements.purpose: Creates ongoing contact between the House and each piece, supports light authentication for secondhand pieces, and keeps a story archive that feeds content.
candidate_elements.reason: The selection already folds the record and dated label into C4. Keeping it lean, as a fitting ledger rather than a resale passport, preserves provenance value without the heavy platform build or a resale business.

candidate_elements.element: Resale or certified pre-owned circuit run by Dior
candidate_elements.purpose: Would turn returned pieces into a controlled second-hand market.
candidate_elements.reason: It risks cannibalizing new sales, makes pre-owned too visible, and moves the campaign toward transaction and infrastructure. Second Fitting is about keeping a piece, not selling it on.

candidate_elements.element: Public pop-up atelier that repairs garments from any brand
candidate_elements.purpose: Would create a surprising, generous press moment and reach people who do not own Dior.
candidate_elements.reason: It adds cost, liability and exclusivity dilution, and it pulls attention from Dior's own pieces. The story-sharing it relies on is already served by real client transformations.

candidate_elements.element: Open fitting sessions where the public watches the petites mains work and meets the owner
candidate_elements.purpose: Keeps C1's best quality, human generosity and live craft, inside the Dior-only scope, and makes the atelier a visible protagonist.
candidate_elements.reason: A small version (live fittings in selected boutiques and a Paris atelier moment) strengthens the craft-credit story and the press hook without repairing other brands' clothes. It is scoped to Dior pieces to protect quality control.

candidate_elements.element: Present-tense transformation stories (new body, new job, new city, a piece restyled for a younger wearer, not just inherited)
candidate_elements.purpose: Counters the heirloom and nostalgia risk and makes the idea relevant to younger audiences and to people whose lives are changing now.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief's central risk is that the idea feels old. Leading with change in the present, with inheritance as one of several chapters, keeps the platform fresh and widely relatable.

candidate_elements.element: Published service promise (turnaround times, pricing tiers, capacity per boutique) established before launch
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes the promise believable and avoids a gap between the advertising and the experience.
candidate_elements.reason: Atelier capacity is the largest threat to credibility. A clear, staged rollout (starting with a few ateliers and iconic pieces such as the Bar jacket and Lady Dior) protects the promise and supports the status of the service.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an optional signature mend finish (Dior motif) as one of the choices within a Second Fitting.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It captures the visual, shareable strength of C3 and gives owners a way to personalize, without making visible repair the central idea or glamorizing damage.

revisions_after_selection.change: Specified that story selection leads with present-tense change (a new body, role or city, a piece restyled for a younger wearer), with inheritance as one chapter among several.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It reduces the risk of a nostalgic, heirloom-only tone and widens appeal to younger audiences.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined the record of fittings as a lean client ledger tied to the dated, signed label, with a light authentication check for secondhand pieces.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the useful provenance and ongoing-relationship value of C2 and addresses brand-control concerns without resale infrastructure.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added live fitting moments in selected boutiques, scoped to Dior pieces only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives the idea a visible, human, press-worthy experience in the spirit of C1 while avoiding cost, liability and dilution from repairing other brands.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a staged rollout with a published service promise (turnaround, pricing, capacity) before launch.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The idea fails if the atelier cannot deliver. A realistic, scoped promise protects credibility and keeps the service feeling exclusive.

final_proposal.title: Second Fitting
final_proposal.idea: Dior was built on the first fitting: the moment a piece is made for one body. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be re-fitted for the life its owner is living now: a Bar jacket let out for a new body, a mother's coat recut for a daughter, a Lady Dior re-edged, perhaps with a small embroidered star over the mend. Each piece returns with a dated, signed label naming the hands that worked on it. The campaign tells real transformations, led by change in the present, through film, live boutique fittings, a client ledger and press. Keeping a Dior becomes the new status act.
follow_up_questions: What would a Second Fitting look like for someone who has never owned a Dior piece, and how could the House welcome a secondhand owner without diluting exclusivity?
Which life changes beyond inheritance (a new job, a changing body, a move, a reinvention) could become the most resonant and least nostalgic chapters of the story?
How could the signed label turn the petites mains into recognizable names, and what would it mean for them to become the faces of the House's commitment to longevity?

focus_check.core_direction: Dior offers a signed, visible atelier mend, a 'second signature' in its own language of thread, needle and hand, that makes a repaired piece more valuable and more personal than an untouched one.

required_elements.what_it_does: Resolves the clash with Dior's polish and perfection. Repair stays open to everyone, and the signed mend remains a choice, which keeps it desirable.

required_elements.what_it_does: Prevents the idea from romanticising damage or becoming a distressed-look trend, and keeps the mark authentic and credible.

final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into a second signature. When a cherished piece, such as a Bar jacket, a Saddle bag or a Lady Dior, returns to the atelier, the owner chooses: an invisible mend, or a signed one. The signed mend uses the couture tacking stitch, normally hidden, left visible and signed by the named petite main who made it. Only what is needed is repaired. The creases and patina of a lived life stay. The campaign photographs these mends with the reverence of a runway look: macro portraits of thread, and owners telling the story behind each piece. It launches as a waiting-list capsule of icons. The signed mend becomes something money cannot buy new: proof of time, wear and care. A Dior piece is not finished when it is bought. It is finished when it has been lived in.

final_proposal.title: Frame the First One
final_proposal.idea: Direct deposit made the first paycheck vanish. What used to be an envelope you held and showed someone is now a number in an app. Canva gives the moment its ritual back with a First Paycheck keepsake: a distinctive, frameable page showing the date, the job, what you did that week and who you told first. The amount is optional and can be hidden, because the number is private, but the milestone isn't. It works for teens, graduates, career changers and late starters, and for any first one, however it went. It can grow into a physical frame partnership, an annual first-payday moment and freelancer versions. Later, teams can send new hires a team-signed card, once it solves a real onboarding need.

If a first payday became a yearly shared moment, who else would want to take part and what would they make?

final_proposal.title: Pay Together
final_proposal.idea:
Pay Together is a small gift of money that only works when two people are in the same place. One person sends a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles as a virtual Mastercard in an app. It unlocks only when both people tap their phones together at a local independent venue. The gift is the invitation, so nobody has to say 'I'm lonely, can we meet?'

For people with no one to send it to, Open Tap works with befriending charities and neighbourhood groups, who pass gifts to people they support and match them with a volunteer or neighbour. Gifts stay small, venues stay unbranded, and success is counted in meetings made, not money spent. Pilot in one city with a few cafés and two charities, using a simple tap-to-confirm. It turns Priceless from a slogan into something you can actually use.
follow_up_questions: Which moments, such as a new job, a new baby, a house move or a bereavement, are most naturally opened by a gift that can only be used together?
What would make a gift feel like a warm invitation rather than an obligation, and who should be allowed to send one?
How could Open Tap match strangers so it feels safe, dignified and optional for the person receiving the gift?

final_proposal.title: Line Item: Not in the Job Description
final_proposal.idea: Every first paycheck pays for more than the job title says. Hidden in it is a skill nobody listed: the new hire who rescues the menu, the poster, the pitch or the training deck because they could make it look right. The campaign reveals this 'unlisted line item' on a redesigned first pay stub and celebrates the accidental designer across every industry, from cafés to clinics to construction sites. Canva then turns recognition into action: a skills receipt that makes the hidden talent visible, and an impact one-pager for reviews, raises or team shout-outs. Managers get a template to spot unlisted skills in new hires. New line items, roles and career stages keep the format running, and it positions design as an everyday work skill for everyone.

final_proposal.title: First Paid
final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck. Everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. First Paid turns that memory into a receipt. People choose the design that earned their first money, add the date and who paid them, and decide whether to show the amount, which is hidden by default. writing_notes.intended_reader: The reader is a senior marketing or brand lead at Dior, or an agency colleague, who knows the house, its history and the sustainability conversation in luxury. They have not seen the four earlier directions and need to grasp the chosen idea quickly, then decide whether to develop it further.

reader_needs.point: What the idea is, in one clear sentence: people submit a garment they cannot let go of, and the atelier remakes some of them into couture.
reader_needs.why: If the reader cannot repeat the idea after one read, it cannot be taken forward or defended in a meeting.

reader_needs.point: Why the New Look's 80th anniversary is the right moment and how the idea inverts 1947.
reader_needs.why: The anniversary is the cultural hook that gives Dior a credible reason to speak about reuse now.

reader_needs.point: That the couture remakes are the showcase and sit alongside a wider repair and alteration service in boutiques.
reader_needs.why: This answers the obvious objection that the idea is elitist or greenwashing, and it ties the campaign to real repair and reuse behaviour.

reader_needs.point: How the campaign unfolds, from submissions and films to the closing show with original owners.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs to see a hero moment and a platform, not only a concept.

terms_to_explain.explanation: Christian Dior's first collection in 1947, with nipped waists and full skirts using generous amounts of fabric. It launched the house and was a celebration of abundance after wartime shortage.
The atelier takes a customer's existing garment and transforms it by hand into a new one-of-a-kind piece, keeping part of the original material and its memory.
A wider, everyday offer of repair and alteration in Dior boutiques for Dior pieces, so more people benefit than the few couture remakes.

tone_choices.choice: Confident and plain, with no jargon or marketing buzzwords.
tone_choices.reason: A busy reader should be able to understand the idea at first pass, and plain language suits an idea about honesty and what already exists.

tone_choices.choice: Lead with the human image of owners wearing their remade garments, not with sustainability claims.
tone_choices.reason: The emotion is what makes the idea distinctive, and it avoids sounding like a greenwashing statement.

tone_choices.choice: Name the boutique service alongside the couture remakes in the same breath.
tone_choices.reason: It shows the idea is credible and honest about its scope, which builds trust with a sceptical reader.

outline: Title and the idea in one sentence.
The inversion: what the New Look did in 1947 and what Dior says now.
How it works: submit a garment and its story, the atelier selects and remakes.
The documented process and the closing show with original owners.
The boutique repair and alteration tier launched at the same time.
Why this is distinctly Dior.

clarity_checks.check: The idea can be understood from the first two sentences.
clarity_checks.how: Read only the opening lines and confirm they state what people do and what Dior does in return.

clarity_checks.check: Every term a non-specialist might not know is explained in context.
clarity_checks.how: Scan for New Look, remake and service tier, and make sure each is clear without a footnote.

clarity_checks.check: The text stays within 150 words and has no filler.
clarity_checks.how: Count the words of the idea and cut any sentence that does not add a fact or a reason.

clarity_checks.check: The three questions are open and useful for further thinking.
clarity_checks.how: Check that none can be answered with yes or no and that each points to a different area of development.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a repair and alteration service tier in boutiques, launched on the same day as the call for submissions.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The concern about elitism and greenwashing is only answered if everyday repair of Dior pieces is part of the idea from the start.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set eligibility rules: a limited number of non-Dior garments can enter the couture selection, while the service tier is for Dior pieces only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It settles the question of what can be submitted and keeps the service focused on Dior's own products and repair behaviour.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a discreet signature mark from C4 and a provenance record from C1 on each remade piece.
revisions_after_selection.reason: They make the remakes recognisable and give each piece a history, without needing the heavy infrastructure of a full Lineage system.

revisions_after_selection.change: Phased the work: call for submissions, selection and filming first, with the show as culmination and the service continuing afterwards.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It manages the limited lead time before the anniversary and keeps the campaign going after the show.

revisions_after_selection.change: Moved the atelier skills content from C2 into a supporting role as short films within the process documentary.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It humanises the petites mains and adds craft knowledge without turning the campaign into a teaching programme.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior's New Look answered scarcity with abundance. For its 80th anniversary, Dior says the new luxury is what already exists. People submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture pieces, filmed from first cut to final fitting. Each carries a discreet Dior mark and a record of its past. The anniversary show closes with the owners wearing their remade pieces. On the same day, Dior boutiques launch a repair and alteration service for Dior pieces, so the idea reaches beyond couture. Craft, memory and reuse become one act of reinvention, which is what Dior has always done best.
follow_up_questions: What would make a person choose a garment to submit, and how could the story they tell become the heart of the content?
How could the boutique repair service feel as special as a couture fitting while being open to many more people?
What happens after the show: how could the remade pieces and their owners keep the idea alive for years?

required_elements.element: A before-and-after payslip redesign that is visual, plain-language and descriptive only (what each line is, never advice)
required_elements.what_it_does: Delivers the central proof of 'design is clarity' in one image, solves deduction shock, and stays clear of financial-guidance risk.

required_elements.element: Employer and payroll templates in Canva for Teams, plus a small pilot group of employers or providers
required_elements.what_it_does: Creates the B2B route and commercial outcome (template adoption, Teams sign-ups), and puts the redesigned payslip in front of real new hires.

required_elements.element: A privacy-first individual route: restyle your own payslip with redaction built in, working independently of employers

required_elements.element: A keepsake and share layer that turns the clear payslip into a first-paycheck memento

required_elements.element: A clear platform line and expansion path (tax statements, benefits, pension, bonus letters) under 'making the confusing clear'
required_elements.what_it_does: Turns a single payslip stunt into a multi-year B2B platform.

Sequence the rollout in three steps: launch a free template and a public before-and-after reveal, pilot with a few employers or payroll providers who put it in their onboarding, then extend the format to other confusing work documents. Build in guardrails from day one: descriptive copy reviewed by a payroll or tax expert, local-variant templates by market, and redaction applied before any export or share.

borrowed_elements.why_needed: The redesign solves the practical tension, but the first paycheck is also an emotional milestone. A shareable, amount-free keepsake gives the idea a celebratory social moment and a natural sharing mechanic without weakening the B2B clarity focus.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set a launch sequence: free template and public reveal, then employer and provider pilots, then expansion to other documents.

final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck should be a milestone, not a puzzle. Canva redesigns the payslip so it explains itself: a visual flow from gross to take-home, with every deduction described in one plain sentence and no advice. Employers and payroll providers adopt it through Canva for Teams templates and put it in their onboarding. New earners can restyle their own payslip, with sensitive numbers redacted by default, and turn it into a keepsake, with an optional thank-you to whoever helped them get there. final_proposal.title: The Paycheck, Explained
final_proposal.idea: Pay stubs are among the most important and least designed documents of adult life. Canva redesigns the first-paycheck experience, turning the gross-to-net shock into a clear, friendly visual story. A hero film follows a first-time earner opening a confusing stub and watching it become something they understand. Around it sit makeover reveals, creator explainers and OOH that mimics ugly pay stubs. Free templates let first-timers decode their pay and let HR teams and small business owners welcome new hires with a clear explainer, a personal note and a team shout-out. All examples use fictional data and explain rather than advise. The platform: 'Design is how things make sense.'

final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into hems for luck. Now, every Dior piece that returns to the atelier for repair or restyling is finished with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in its lining, signed by the artisan who mended it. The mark cannot be bought, licensed or put on anything new; it can only be earned by keeping a piece alive. A light repair log travels with the piece into resale, so its mended life adds to its value. Irreparable pieces are reborn as small keepsakes that still earn the sprig. writing_notes.intended_reader: The reader is a Dior marketing or sustainability lead, or a client-side creative partner, who knows the house, its history and the luxury category well. They know the repair and reuse brief, but they have not seen the four candidate directions or the selection reasoning, and they will judge the idea quickly, mainly on whether it is ownable and workable.

reader_needs.point: What the idea is: a hand-embroidered muguet sprig added to any Dior piece that is repaired or restyled in the atelier.
reader_needs.why: If the reader cannot picture the mark and the moment it is given, nothing else in the proposal will land.

reader_needs.point: Why it belongs only to Dior, because it comes from Christian Dior's own lily of the valley superstition.
reader_needs.why: Ownability is the main reason this idea beats a generic sustainability gesture.

reader_needs.point: How it changes behaviour: the sprig is never sold, so visible wear becomes an earned status mark instead of a shame.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs to see that the idea works through luxury values and not through guilt.

reader_needs.point: How the main risks are handled: atelier capacity, the gimmick risk and pieces that cannot be repaired.
reader_needs.why: A credible plan for the weak points lets the reader trust the idea enough to take it forward.

terms_to_explain.explanation: The French word for lily of the valley, the small white flower Christian Dior treated as his lucky charm.
The Dior workshop where artisans make and mend garments by hand.
Reworking an existing piece, for example by altering its cut or length, so that it can be worn again in a new way.

tone_choices.choice: Write in a confident, warm and plain voice with short sentences.
tone_choices.reason: A busy reader should grasp the idea in one pass, and the tone should suit a house that values restraint.

tone_choices.choice: Describe repair as devotion and continuation, and avoid guilt-based or moralising sustainability language.
tone_choices.reason: Luxury clients respond to desire and heritage, and the idea's strength is that it never lectures.

tone_choices.choice: Name concrete details such as the hem, the lining, the artisan's name and the fallback keepsake, and avoid abstract campaign vocabulary.
tone_choices.reason: Specific images make the idea believable and show that it can be delivered.

outline: Open with the founder's superstition of sewing lily of the valley into hems for luck.
State the idea: the muguet sprig as the finishing mark for every repaired or restyled piece, signed by the artisan.
Explain the rule that makes it work: the sprig is never sold, licensed or put on new pieces.
Show the behaviour shift: wear becomes a badge of devotion, and second-hand owners can earn it too.
Cover delivery: a phased rollout from couture and iconic pieces, and a keepsake for pieces that cannot be saved.
Close with how far the mark can travel, ending on one recognisable image.

clarity_checks.check: The text claims nothing that contradicts itself.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Repairs may be paid for, so 'can't be bought' could be challenged. The strict rule is that the sprig is never sold as an object or used for anything except repair, which keeps it credible.

revisions_after_selection.change: Extended eligibility to Dior pieces bought second-hand.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This connects the idea to resale, so the mark supports reuse across several owners and not only the first buyer.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a phased rollout, starting with couture and iconic pieces.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It protects the quality and atelier capacity that the idea depends on.

revisions_after_selection.reason: No client should leave empty-handed, and the fallback removes a gap in the original concept.

revisions_after_selection.change: Specified that the artisan signs the work by name, as a consistent part of the ritual and not an optional extra.

final_proposal.title: Lucky Thread
final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into the hems of his dresses for luck. Lucky Thread revives that ritual for repair. Whenever a Dior piece returns to the atelier to be mended or restyled, an artisan finishes it with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining and signs the work with their name. The sprig is never sold, licensed or added to new pieces, so the only way to have one is to keep a Dior piece in use. That turns a mended hem from something to hide into a mark of devotion, and it works for pieces bought second-hand too. It begins with couture and iconic pieces, then widens as the atelier grows. If a piece cannot be saved, the atelier reinterprets it into a keepsake that carries the sprig. One small stitch, recognisable in a single image.
follow_up_questions: What other hidden parts of a garment, such as the lining, the hem or the inside label, could become the most treasured part of a piece?
If the sprig can only be earned and never bought, what else in Dior's history could be given through devotion and not through purchase?
How should the house recognise a piece that has been mended many times: with a name, a number of chapters, or a story told by its owners?

element_review.selected_core_idea: Mastercard admits that the fastest payment ever quietly removed one of the last small human exchanges of the day, and gives merchants and customers a simple way to slow the tap down so that a minute of unhurried time becomes the new Priceless.

candidate_elements.element: A pilot built on a committed group of independent merchants in a few neighbourhoods, run during set 'Slow Hours' when queues are short
candidate_elements.purpose: Make sure the idea is real on the ground and not a gimmick. It also answers the queue and busy-shop concerns by choosing when and where the idea works.
candidate_elements.reason: Merchant participation is the idea's biggest risk. A small, committed, well-supported start gives believable proof and photogenic stories before any scale-up.

candidate_elements.element: An open admission in the brand voice that speed had a cost, with Mastercard taking responsibility for giving some time back
candidate_elements.purpose: Pre-empt the challenge 'isn't Mastercard the reason things got faster?' and make the campaign credible.
candidate_elements.reason: The candour is what separates the idea from opportunism. It is part of the insight and costs nothing.

candidate_elements.element: A one-line, optional conversation prompt on the counter signal (for example 'Ask me about today's bake')
candidate_elements.purpose: Remove the awkwardness of what to say after the pause, borrowing the 'low-pressure excuse' logic of C3 without any peer-payment product.
candidate_elements.reason: A pause with nothing to say can feel odd. A light prompt makes the chat easy for shy customers and for merchants, and it is cheap and easy to produce. It stays optional so it never feels scripted.

candidate_elements.element: A free merchant kit (counter signal, sticker, simple how-to) and a standalone sound option for terminals that cannot change their payment sound
candidate_elements.purpose: Make joining almost free and independent of terminal and bank partners, so the idea can launch quickly.
candidate_elements.reason: The core relies on a sonic and visual signal. A fallback means technical limits cannot block the pilot, and it keeps the scale advantage over C3.

candidate_elements.element: A public 'Minutes Given' tally, where merchants and customers log the unhurried minutes
candidate_elements.purpose: Give the campaign a simple measure, a shareable PR number and a sense of collective momentum.
candidate_elements.reason: It makes a soft behaviour measurable and gives the idea a story that grows over time. It stays light and anonymous so nobody is labelled lonely.

candidate_elements.element: A separate programme pairing older adults with young volunteers to learn digital payments
candidate_elements.purpose: Add financial inclusion credibility and intergenerational stories.
candidate_elements.reason: It reads as CSR, is narrow, and risks being patronising. It would shift the idea from a universal, non-stigmatising gesture to a help programme for one group. It could be explored later as a partnership, but it should not be part of the core.

candidate_elements.element: A redeemable 'coffee's on me' credit sent to a drifted friend
candidate_elements.purpose: Give a reason to reconnect with someone you know.
candidate_elements.reason: It depends on bank and app partners, competes with strong P2P products, and serves people who already have contacts. It would also take focus away from the physical moment at the till.

candidate_elements.element: An 'open seat' table marker that invites strangers to dine together
candidate_elements.purpose: Create shared moments between strangers.
candidate_elements.reason: It asks lonely people to take a big social leap and raises safety and consent issues. It also invites comparison with dating and social apps, and it works against the low-pressure simplicity of C1.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the launch as a merchant-first pilot of 'Slow Hours' in a few neighbourhoods with committed independent shops, cafes and markets, instead of a broad rollout.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This tackles the gimmick risk and the queue reality directly, and gives real, repeatable stories to build on.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the brand's admission that speed had a cost a visible part of the campaign voice.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It turns the 'Mastercard made things faster' objection into the source of credibility.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an optional conversation prompt on the counter signal.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the pause easy to fill for shy customers and busy merchants, without scripting the chat.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a standalone sound and signal kit as a fallback where terminals cannot play an 'unhurried' sound.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the idea free of dependence on terminal or bank partners, so it can launch fast and consistently.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light, anonymous 'Minutes Given' tally.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives the campaign a measure and a shareable PR number without asking anyone to identify as lonely.

revisions_after_selection.change: Tempered the claim: the campaign offers a minute of human warmth and does not claim to cure loneliness.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A modest promise is more honest, fits a sensitive topic, and protects the brand from overreach.

final_proposal.title: Take Your Time
final_proposal.idea: The tap made paying instant, and in doing so it deleted the last small conversation in many people's day. Mastercard says so openly, then offers a way back. Independent merchants join with a free counter signal and an optional 'unhurried' payment sound that says 'I've got a minute.' Anyone can opt in by pausing their tap, and the merchant answers with a chat. A one-line prompt on the sign makes starting easy. Nobody has to say they are lonely, because it is for everyone. It starts in committed neighbourhoods during Slow Hours, when the queue is short, and a public 'Minutes Given' tally shows the effect growing. Priceless stops being only the big rare moment and becomes a literal minute of someone's time.
follow_up_questions: What would make a merchant proud to display the signal rather than see it as extra work, and what would they need to keep it going over months?
How could the unhurried sound feel warm and recognisable as Mastercard without becoming irritating when heard dozens of times a day?
Beyond independent shops, where else does speed quietly remove human contact (self-checkout, ticket gates, delivery handovers), and could the pause travel there?

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a clear fallback: if the meetup is not held by the agreed date, the app gently offers a normal payment or a reschedule, with no penalty or guilt.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Meetups may not happen, and the experience must never leave a debt unresolved or make the user feel judged.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the first version a small pilot with a P2P partner and a handful of cafés in one or two cities, with a prototype demo as a backup.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This answers the concern about needing a product partner and gives early real usage as proof, so it does not read as a gimmick.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a measure of success: completed meetups, not transactions avoided.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the idea focused on real human outcomes and gives the client a credible story to tell.

revisions_after_selection.change: Kept the framing as 'time with people' for everyone and removed any language about lonely people.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Avoiding stigma is a core strength, and it widens participation.

final_proposal.title: Owe Me One
final_proposal.idea: We all know the moment: a friend covers your coffee and you say, "I'll get you next time." That small debt is often the reason two people meet again. Owe Me One turns it into a feature. When splitting a bill or repaying a friend, people can choose "Settle in person": instead of sending money, the app sets a shared date to meet. A payments brand choosing not to complete a payment is the provocation. Mastercard moves money, so it can say what money should move us toward: time together, the one thing you can't send digitally. We would start with a pilot with a payment partner and a few local cafés, backed by the social question "Who do you owe one?" If a meetup doesn't happen, the app offers a normal payment, no guilt. Success is counted in meetups held.
follow_up_questions: Who is the one person you keep meaning to see, and what small debt could be the excuse?
Which everyday payment moments, beyond splitting a bill, hide a reason to meet again?
What would make a meetup feel easy and unforced for people who have drifted apart?

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the imposter-to-proof feeling from C4 a tone cue for the creative ('You got paid. You're official.') and not a separate asset kit.

final_proposal.title: The Paycheck, Explained
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck is the most important document you've never been taught to read. Canva publicly redesigns it. Real first-timers (retail, kitchens, warehouses, offices) react to their gross-to-net shock, then see a fictional pay stub transformed into a clear, friendly visual story. Free templates let HR teams and small business owners do the same, plus a First Payday pack with a welcome note, plain-language explainer and team shout-out. OOH mimics ugly, jargon-packed pay stubs. All data is fictional, and it's explanation, never financial advice. The platform: 'Design is how things make sense.'

focus_check.core_purpose: Repair is seen as a chore or a virtue signal, or as a fix for a flaw, so luxury owners rarely seek it out. Dior needs to make repairing and keeping its pieces something existing and aspiring owners want to do and be proud of.
focus_check.core_direction: Turn repair into a Dior signature: a hand-stitched mend based on the cannage lattice, offered as a visible or invisible choice and recorded on a dated card, so a mended piece is a badge of a well-loved Dior.

required_elements.element: A cannage-based mending technique created by the petites mains
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes repair ownable and unmistakably Dior. It separates the idea from generic visible mending and gives the campaign a visual asset.

required_elements.element: Owner's choice between a visible and an invisible mend
required_elements.what_it_does: Keeps repair attractive to every kind of owner and makes the visible mend an act of personal expression, not an obligation.

required_elements.element: Dated card recording the owner's reason for keeping the piece
required_elements.what_it_does: Turns each mend into an emotional story and a record of care. This is what makes the repaired piece feel more valuable.

required_elements.element: Celebration of the most-worn heritage pieces (Bar jacket, Lady Dior) across runway, film, social and boutiques
required_elements.what_it_does: Creates the cultural status flip, from pristine to well-loved. It also gives the platform a reach beyond the service itself.

required_elements.element: Owner-generated sharing of mends
required_elements.what_it_does: Earns attention through pride, not preaching, and spreads the idea beyond the people who own the pieces.

required_elements.element: Guardrails on craft and framing: mends only for wear, always in cannage geometry, signed by the petite main who made them
required_elements.what_it_does: Avoids the kintsugi cliché and any suggestion of celebrating damage. It keeps the focus on care, long ownership and Dior's own craft.

required_elements.element: Phased rollout with stated capacity and turnaround times
required_elements.what_it_does: Protects the promise of couture-level quality and prevents the service becoming a bottleneck if demand spikes.

required_elements.element: A link to reuse: the mend card stays with the piece when it is passed on
required_elements.what_it_does: Covers the 'reuse' half of the brief. A mend adds to a piece's history and value for future owners, so keeping and passing on pieces becomes desirable.

focus_check.development_plan: Make the idea sharper and more feasible in three ways. First, define the technique as a named house craft with strict rules: cannage geometry only, Dior thread palette, and each mend signed by the petite main who made it. Second, start with a pilot on the heritage pieces, the Bar jacket and the Lady Dior, in a few ateliers and boutiques, with published turnaround times, then widen the range of pieces and cities. Third, shift the campaign language from celebrating scuffs to celebrating the most loved and longest worn, with the runway, film and boutique expressions built on real owners' pieces. borrowed_elements.element: Provenance record that travels with the piece through later owners
borrowed_elements.why_needed: The brief covers reuse as well as repair. Letting the dated mend card pass to the next owner means a mend adds to a piece's story and value, which encourages passing pieces on. It does this without building a full resale operation.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Brings reuse into the idea alongside repair, and makes a mended piece more desirable to future owners.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set a phased rollout beginning with heritage pieces and a few ateliers, with published turnaround times.

final_proposal.title: The Cannage Darn
final_proposal.idea: Dior's petites mains develop a hand-stitched mend built from the cannage lattice, the house's most recognisable code. When a well-worn Bar jacket, Lady Dior or other Dior piece comes in for repair, the owner chooses: an invisible mend, or a visible cannage darn that marks a piece that was truly loved. Each mend is signed by the petite main who made it, and the piece returns with a dated card recording why its owner kept it. Rollout is phased, starting with heritage pieces and clear turnaround times.

focus_check.core_purpose: To address loneliness by restoring the small, everyday human contact that frictionless payment has quietly removed, for people whose chat at the till may be one of the few conversations they have in a day, without asking them to say they are lonely.
focus_check.core_direction: Mastercard turns the moment of payment into an optional invitation to an unhurried minute of conversation, using a merchant counter signal and a slower 'no rush' version of its payment sound.

required_elements.element: A recognisable counter mark that merchants display to show they are taking part
required_elements.what_it_does: Shows customers where an unhurried minute is on offer and gives merchants a public commitment, so the idea doesn't depend on chance encounters.

required_elements.element: A slower, unhurried version of the Mastercard payment sound
required_elements.what_it_does: Signals 'no rush, I've got a minute' without words. It makes the idea feel different and is ownable by Mastercard.

required_elements.element: Opt-in by pausing before the tap, with the merchant also able to offer the minute
required_elements.what_it_does: Lets anyone join without labelling themselves as lonely. The merchant's offer helps shy or hesitant customers who would not pause on their own.

required_elements.element: A committed starting set of independent merchants who choose their own 'Take Your Time' hours
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes sure the promise is kept, avoids queue pressure and protects the merchants' business. It also guards against the idea looking like a gimmick.

required_elements.element: Lightweight merchant onboarding (a short guide with simple, natural conversation openers)
required_elements.what_it_does: Helps merchants make the minute feel warm and genuine rather than scripted or awkward, so the exchange reliably delivers human contact.

required_elements.element: An honest brand admission that speed has a cost
required_elements.what_it_does: Answers 'isn't Mastercard the reason things got faster?' by turning candour into credibility, and frames the campaign as giving time back.

required_elements.element: A simple measure of 'minutes given'
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes Priceless tangible and reportable, and gives PR and social a human number without tracking individual conversations.

focus_check.development_plan: Make the idea more concrete and feasible. Define the unit as one minute, and make the counter mark and slower sound the core assets. Launch as a neighbourhood pilot with independent merchants in conversation-friendly businesses (cafés, bakeries, markets, barbers, newsagents, pharmacies), each choosing quieter hours. Build the sound so it can run at the till through a pilot terminal update or a simple counter device, so launch doesn't depend on a full terminal rollout. Add a two-way trigger so merchants can offer the minute as well as customers. Keep all in-store language about time and warmth, and leave the word 'loneliness' to the wider communications, so no customer feels diagnosed. Lead the story with an honest brand admission.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the trigger two-way: customers can pause their tap, and merchants can also offer the slower sound.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Lonely or shy people are the least likely to start the exchange themselves. A merchant's offer lowers the barrier while keeping the idea opt-in and non-stigmatising.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added merchant-chosen 'Take Your Time' hours and a launch limited to committed independent merchants.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This addresses the queue and busy-shop concern directly and makes sure the idea is not a gimmick, because every participating merchant has chosen to take part and can keep the promise.

revisions_after_selection.change: Specified a feasible way to deliver the sound at launch, through a pilot terminal update or a small counter device.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The original idea relied on Mastercard's sonic identity but did not say how it would reach the till. A realistic route lets the pilot start without waiting for an industry-wide terminal change.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a short merchant guide with natural conversation openers.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A minute only works if it feels genuine. Light support helps merchants who are unsure what to say, and makes the experience more consistent across shops.

revisions_after_selection.change: Kept all in-store messaging about time and warmth, and removed any mention of loneliness at the till.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Naming loneliness in the shop would label customers and undermine the main strength of the idea, which is that nobody has to self-identify.

revisions_after_selection.change: Opened the campaign narrative with an explicit admission that speed has a cost.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The 'Mastercard made things faster' challenge is the idea's biggest credibility risk. Admitting it first makes the brand believable and turns the challenge into the reason the campaign exists.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added 'minutes given' as the headline measure.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the Priceless idea tangible and easy to communicate, and it counts what is offered without monitoring or commercialising private conversations.

final_proposal.title: Take Your Time
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying take about a second, and in doing so quietly deleted the last small conversation in many people's day. Take Your Time gives some of it back. Independent shops, cafés and markets display a counter mark and, during hours they choose, offer a slower, unhurried version of the Mastercard sound at the till. It means: no rush, I've got a minute. Customers join by pausing before they tap, and merchants can offer the minute too, so nobody has to say they're lonely. It starts as a neighbourhood pilot with committed independent merchants, scheduled around quiet hours to avoid queues, and it opens by admitting plainly what speed cost us. Priceless stops being a rare, big experience and becomes a literal minute of someone's time, counted and shared by the places that give it.
follow_up_questions: Where else has convenience removed a small human exchange (self-checkout, delivery, ride apps), and could a brand give time back there?
What would make a merchant proud to carry the mark and the sound, and what would make a customer seek it out or recognise it in the wild?
How can success be measured honestly, for example through minutes given, without turning a human conversation into a KPI?

final_proposal.title: First Stub
final_proposal.idea: The first paycheck is the moment work becomes real, yet the document that carries it is often the ugliest paper of early working life. First Stub is Canva's redesign of the pay stub as a clear, human one-page story: hours shown as a visual timeline, deductions labelled in plain language, and a personal note from the manager at the top. reader_needs.why: If the reader cannot picture it in one breath, they will not be able to judge or retell it.

reader_needs.point: Mastercard is credible here because it built its reputation on speed and is now saying speed is not always the point.
reader_needs.why: This tension is what makes the idea surprising and keeps the link to loneliness from feeling borrowed.

reader_needs.point: The lane is for everyone, so nobody has to identify as lonely or be pitied.
reader_needs.why: It is the main reason the idea avoids the stigma problems of the other directions.

reader_needs.point: It starts as a measured pilot and grows only if it is sustained, recognises cashiers and publishes results.
reader_needs.why: The reader's main worries will be throughput cost and the risk of a stunt, so the proposal must show those risks are managed.

terms_to_explain.explanation: An optional setting on the payment terminal that replaces the quick confirmation beep with a softer sound and a short pause. It does not slow the payment network itself.

The effort of managing feelings and being warm with customers as part of a job. The idea must recognise it and never assume it is free.

tone_choices.reason: The idea is about human pace, so the text should read at a human pace and be easy for a busy reader to follow.

tone_choices.reason: The brand's honesty is the hook, and it keeps the proposal from sounding like a generic awareness campaign.

tone_choices.choice: Be candid about the risks and say what answers them, without overclaiming that the idea cures loneliness.
tone_choices.reason: A sober tone builds trust with a reader who will be looking for flaws, and it respects a sensitive subject.

The human truth: for some people the checkout is the only conversation of the day.
The idea: one unhurried lane, marked with a sign, staffed by cashiers who opt in, open to everyone.
The brand assets: the acceptance mark, the terminal and an optional Slow Tap with a warmer sound.
How it starts and grows: a measured pilot at quieter times, recognition for cashiers, published results, then Slow Hour and Slow Day.
Why it is a movement and not a stunt: sustained commitment and honest measurement.

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying faster. Now it says: not everything should be. The Slow Lane is one checkout lane in partner grocers, pharmacies and markets, marked 'This lane takes its time.' Cashiers choose to staff it, are recognised for it and have time to chat. Anyone can use it, so nobody has to say they're lonely. For some people the till is the only conversation of their day, and this meets them there. An optional 'Slow Tap' mode on the terminal swaps the efficient beep for a warmer sound and a short pause. A sustained programme is what makes it a movement, not a stunt.

final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. element_review.selected_core_idea: A tiny hand-embroidered lily of the valley (muguet) sprig, drawn from Christian Dior's hem superstition, is sewn into the lining of every piece repaired or restyled by the atelier. It can't be bought, only earned by keeping a piece alive, which turns repair into a status-bearing ritual.

candidate_elements.element: Lineage record of repairs: a light digital and physical log in which each muguet sprig is recorded with the date, the artisan's name and a short note from the owner
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes the earned mark verifiable and traceable. It supports resale trust and authentication, gives the house first-party data on how long pieces live, and lets the sprig count become a visible life story.
candidate_elements.reason: It strengthens the promise that the mark is never sold, because each sprig is tied to a real repair. It also fills the plan for resale and the archive. It is kept as a thin supporting layer (a record of repairs, not a full ownership-passport platform), so the tactile muguet ritual remains the lead and the idea does not become tech-led.

candidate_elements.element: Public launch moment: a short-run atelier repair salon at 30 Montaigne where the first sprigs are embroidered live and the artisans are introduced by name
candidate_elements.purpose: Creates a launch spectacle that shows the hand skill, builds press and social attention, and demonstrates the ritual before the system rolls out.
candidate_elements.reason: It gives Lucky Thread a visible start and makes the artisan credit tangible. It is limited to Dior clients' own pieces, so it avoids the C4 concerns about mending other brands' garments, diluting exclusivity and turning into a one-off stunt. It is positioned as the opening of the system, not the idea itself.

candidate_elements.element: Fallback for irreparable pieces: the atelier reinterprets the garment into a smaller object, or keeps a fragment as an archival keepsake, and still embroiders the muguet
candidate_elements.purpose: Ensures no client leaves empty-handed and addresses the stated concern about pieces that can't be repaired.
candidate_elements.reason: It protects the credibility of 'earned by keeping a piece alive', since a restyled keepsake is still the piece continuing. It also adds emotional stories to the content.

candidate_elements.element: Phased rollout: begin with couture and iconic lines (e.g. Bar jacket, Lady Dior), then widen to ready-to-wear and accessories as atelier capacity grows
candidate_elements.purpose: Protects stitch quality and artisan capacity and builds scarcity and desire while the system scales.
candidate_elements.reason: Atelier capacity is the main operational risk. Phasing gives a credible way to scale without compromising the craft or promising what the house cannot yet deliver.

candidate_elements.element: Capsule of reworked pieces built from deadstock and archive offcuts, with visible seams
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds a runway and design-led expression of reuse.
candidate_elements.reason: It shifts attention from clients' own pieces to a limited collection, brings back the greenwashing and trend-imitation risk, and does not support the earned-mark behaviour at the heart of Lucky Thread.

candidate_elements.element: Open-to-any-brand mending service
candidate_elements.purpose: Extends reach to non-clients and builds goodwill.
candidate_elements.reason: It would weaken the idea that the mark is earned by keeping a Dior piece alive, and it raises capacity and exclusivity problems.

candidate_elements.element: Resale authentication tie-in where Dior-certified resale partners recognise the sprig as a mark of care
candidate_elements.purpose: Links repair to resale value, so mending is seen as an investment.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a useful later step but would risk ceding control of the resale market and complicates the launch. The lineage record already leaves room for it, so it is held for a later phase.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light lineage record linking each muguet sprig to a dated repair and a named artisan.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the unbuyable mark verifiable and strengthens the resale and archive story without turning the idea into a tech platform.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an atelier repair salon at 30 Montaigne for Dior pieces only, as the launch moment.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives the system a visible start and puts the artisans' hands and names in front of the public, while avoiding the exclusivity and one-off problems of C4.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined a fallback for irreparable pieces: reinterpretation or an archival keepsake, still finished with the muguet.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It answers the concern about pieces that can't be repaired and keeps the promise that no client is turned away empty-handed.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set a phased rollout from couture and iconic lines to wider ranges, with the sprig strictly unlicensed and never sold.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It protects quality and capacity and keeps the mark credible, so it doesn't read as a gimmick.

final_proposal.title: Lucky Thread
final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into hems for luck. Now, every Dior piece that returns to the atelier for repair or restyling receives a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in its lining. It can't be bought, only earned by keeping a piece alive. Wear becomes a badge, and repair becomes a collectible ritual. The mending artisan is credited by name, and each sprig is logged in a light lineage record that follows the piece into resale and the archive. It launches with a live embroidery salon at 30 Montaigne, then rolls out from couture and icons to wider ranges. Pieces beyond repair are reborn as an atelier keepsake, still marked with the muguet.
follow_up_questions: How could the sprig count and placement become a quiet, recognisable language of devotion that clients and collectors read in the lining of a Dior piece, without ever becoming a logo?
What would the house need to promise, and refuse to do, to keep the mark credibly unbuyable as demand grows, and how should that promise be told publicly?
Beyond the client, who else could carry the ritual (the artisans, the runway, the archive), and what story would each tell about a piece that was kept alive?

final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns the mend into a mark of status. Owners of iconic pieces can choose an invisible repair or a signed one: a hand-stitched mend in Dior's own thread and atelier mark, signed by the petite main who made it. Scuffs, creases and patina are kept; only what is needed is repaired. The campaign photographs these marks with runway reverence through macro imagery and editorials, and tells real owners' stories of the lives behind them. It launches with the Bar jacket, Saddle bag and Lady Dior and a waiting list. Resale platforms can sell a bag, but only Dior can add its second signature, so a repaired piece becomes more desirable than a flawless one.

Where else could a visible mend appear on the runway or in a creative director's collection, so the inversion shows up in new product as well as in repairs?

candidate_elements.element: Broader boutique repair and alteration tier for Dior pieces, announced alongside the couture remakes
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes the campaign credible and gives it reach beyond the few couture remakes. It turns the emotion of the showcase into an everyday repair and reuse behaviour for Dior owners, which is what the client's brief on repair and reuse needs.
candidate_elements.reason: Without it, the idea risks being read as elitist or greenwashing. It is the main fix for the weakest point of C3 and must launch at the same moment, so couture is the showcase and not the whole offer.

candidate_elements.element: Optional signature repair mark stitched into remade and repaired pieces
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives every remade or repaired piece a recognisable, collectable Dior detail. It makes the work visible in the show, in the films and on the street.
candidate_elements.reason: It adds a distinctive visual signature for the campaign and a reason to repair. It stays optional, because some clients prefer invisible mending, and it is a detail of the remakes, not the lead idea, which avoids the borrowed-kintsugi risk.

candidate_elements.element: Provenance record for each remade garment, capturing the owner's story and the atelier's work
candidate_elements.purpose: Records the story of each piece and adds authenticity and long-term loyalty value. It extends the garment-as-memory theme beyond the show.
candidate_elements.reason: A light version supports the campaign without the heavy data build of the full Lineage system. It is limited to the remade pieces and the owner's consent, so the privacy and infrastructure concerns stay small.

candidate_elements.element: Full lifetime provenance system and resale or pass-on registry for all Dior products
candidate_elements.purpose: Would create a long-term authentication and loyalty infrastructure across the whole range.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a heavy operational build, raises privacy questions and could push people towards resale over repair. It is a later layer, not part of this campaign.

candidate_elements.element: Atelier skills content: short films and a few small workshops showing how artisans repair, reline and re-stitch
candidate_elements.purpose: Humanises the petites mains and gives the documentary films a teaching angle. It spreads repair knowledge to a wider audience at low cost.
candidate_elements.reason: As supporting content within the documentary series, it enriches the story and credits the artisans. It stays secondary, so the mystique of the house is kept and it does not become a charity-style programme.

candidate_elements.element: Public pop-up workshop programme in multiple cities open to any brand's garments
candidate_elements.purpose: Would build a skills community and earned media in several cities.
candidate_elements.reason: It is hard to scale, does not drive repair of Dior's own pieces and risks diluting exclusivity. Films carry the skills content instead.

candidate_elements.element: Clear eligibility rules: a limited number of non-Dior garments accepted for the couture selection, Dior-only for the boutique service tier
candidate_elements.purpose: Settles the question of which garments qualify and keeps the campaign open and generous at the couture level without Dior servicing other brands at scale.
candidate_elements.reason: The couture selection is about the story, so the garment's brand matters less. The service tier is about Dior's own products and the client's repair and reuse behaviour.

candidate_elements.element: Phased timeline: open call, selection, filmed remakes, anniversary show, then an exhibition and the continuing service tier
candidate_elements.purpose: Manages the limited lead time and keeps the campaign alive before and after the show.
candidate_elements.reason: It turns the show into a culmination, not a one-off, and makes sure the service tier outlasts the anniversary.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture, filmed from first cut to final fitting, with an optional Dior repair mark and a record of the piece's story. The anniversary show closes with the remade pieces worn by their original owners. On the same day, Dior boutiques launch a repair and alteration service for Dior pieces, so the couture remakes are the showcase, not the whole offer. A limited number of non-Dior garments can enter the couture selection. Atelier films show how the petites mains work, and an exhibition keeps the stories alive after the show.
follow_up_questions: How should the selection of garments be made, and who should choose, so that the stories feel real and varied and not curated for effect?
What would make the boutique repair tier feel like a luxury service, in price, speed and ritual, and not a concession to sustainability?
Beyond the show, what lasting proof could Dior offer, such as numbers of garments repaired or kept in use, to show that this is a behaviour change and not a one-night gesture?

required_elements.element: Slow Lane: a designated, clearly signed checkout lane at partner grocers, pharmacies and markets, open to everyone
required_elements.what_it_does: Puts the intervention where lonely people already are, so nobody has to join anything, identify as lonely or be matched with a stranger.

required_elements.element: Opt-in cashiers who are given protected time and recognition
required_elements.what_it_does: Makes the conversation genuine rather than scripted, and stops the idea from relying on unpaid emotional labour.

required_elements.element: Slow Tap terminal mode and sonic signature
required_elements.what_it_does: Uses Mastercard's own assets to signal that this moment is allowed to take time, and gives the idea a distinctive, ownable sensory cue.

required_elements.what_it_does: Answers merchant throughput concerns, and gives evidence on basket size, repeat visits and staff and customer wellbeing.

required_elements.what_it_does: Separates a lasting movement from a one-off stunt and makes cashiers visible heroes.

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard built its name on making payment fast. Now it says something unexpected: not everything should be. In partner grocers, pharmacies and markets, one checkout lane is set aside as unhurried, under a sign that reads 'This lane takes its time.' It is open to anyone, so nobody has to admit to being lonely. Cashiers opt in, are trained and recognised as Slow Lane hosts, and get the time to chat. An optional 'Slow Tap' mode swaps the efficient beep for a warmer pause. The pilot runs in quieter hours with published results on wellbeing and repeat visits, then grows into Slow Hour, Slow Day and a sonic signature. It meets people in the one place where, for many, a conversation already happens.

What would a Slow Lane sound like, and could a sonic cue become as recognisable as the Mastercard melody while signalling warmth rather than speed?

final_proposal.idea: Loneliness rarely asks for company, but it can say yes to a treat. Tap Together lets anyone send an 'On Me' invitation to a coffee, a haircut, a cinema seat or a bowl of noodles at a local business. If a date doesn't work, the sender is nudged to suggest another. Pilots start in a few cities, with charity partners helping isolated people receive invitations, and results are reported as shared visits.

final_proposal.title: First Paid: The Work Behind the First Paycheck
final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck. They remember what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. 'First Paid' turns that memory into a receipt. People upload the design that earned their first money, add the date and who paid them, and choose whether to show the amount, blurred by default. Each receipt joins a public gallery of work that started careers, and can be shared and tagged to the person who paid. Before launch, we seed it with creators, Canva staff and known figures. 'Work' is defined broadly, from résumés to posters, with a 'first thing I made for someone' entry for those whose first pay did not come from design. 'Made in Canva' stops being a watermark and becomes a badge of a career beginning, and gives teams proof of what people build.

What would make someone proud enough to tag the person who paid them, and what would make them hesitate?

Merchants choose when they have a minute, show a simple counter mark, and the customer opts in by pausing their tap. The sonic identity becomes a supporting cue and is no longer the core mechanic.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A slowed payment sound can look like a gimmick, or like a technical fault and a tax on queues. Putting the choice with the merchant and the customer makes the idea about people rather than technology. It also lowers the risk of friction in busy shops.

revisions_after_selection.reason: This answers the 'isn't Mastercard the reason things got faster?' challenge head on. Candour turns the biggest credibility risk into the reason to believe.

revisions_after_selection.change: Narrowed the launch to a committed group of independent cafes, markets, newsagents and corner shops, running in quiet-hour windows and in a few chosen neighbourhoods before any wider rollout.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This guarantees real merchant participation, avoids queue pressure, and builds proof and stories before the idea scales.

revisions_after_selection.change: Removed any loneliness language from the in-store experience. Loneliness is addressed only in campaign communication and partnerships, never at the till.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Customers should never feel labelled. The idea works because everyone can join without self-identifying, so the till has to stay warm and neutral.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded the best part of C2 (trust and inclusion) in as a supporting merchant programme: merchants get simple guidance on unhurried conversation, and older or less confident payers are welcomed at the slow tap.

final_proposal.title: Take Your Time
final_proposal.idea: Contactless made paying instant, and for many people it quietly removed the last small conversation of their day. Take Your Time gives some of it back. Independent cafes, markets and corner shops display a simple Mastercard counter mark that means 'I've got a minute.' A customer who wants to join just pauses before tapping, and the merchant answers with a chat. A softer, unhurried version of the Mastercard sound marks the moment. Nobody has to say they're lonely, and anyone can take part. Mastercard openly admits the cost of speed and turns Priceless into the smallest, most human form of itself: a minute of someone's time. It launches with committed local merchants in quiet-hour windows, then grows through signage, sound, PR and social.
follow_up_questions: What would make a merchant feel proud, rather than burdened, to offer a minute, and how could Mastercard reward that without turning kindness into a transaction?
How could the unhurried sound and counter mark become a cultural shorthand people recognise and use beyond Mastercard's own channels?
Where else has a convenience quietly removed a small human moment, and could the same 'give the minute back' logic extend to those places?

final_proposal.idea: Most people aren't short of friends. They've just left it too long, and the first message feels awkward. Overdue turns the most dreaded piece of financial mail into an invitation. You list people you owe a catch-up, and your banking app sends a mock notice: 'Amount due: one coffee, one catch-up. final_proposal.title: Paid For This
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck was never really about the number. It was proof that someone valued something you made. 'Paid for this' flips the usual payslip photo and celebrates the work itself: the menu, pitch deck, flyer, logo, rota or slide that earned it. The amount stays hidden, and people pair the work with a feeling or a story. A Canva keepsake template makes it easy to share. Real first-work stories from creators, small-business owners and interns seed the campaign in OOH and a short series. Employers can give new hires a 'Paid for this' welcome card, and first-invoice and Teams tools offer a next step. Canva becomes the place where work worth being paid for gets made.

candidate_elements.element: A boutique repair and alteration service tier, announced at the same moment as the couture remakes
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes reuse available to many more people than the few couture selections reach. It answers the elitism and greenwashing risk and gives the brief a lasting behaviour (repair and reuse of Dior pieces) beyond the anniversary.

candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the couture remakes and service-tier repairs a recognisable, collectable signature and a visual shorthand for the campaign. It lets owners show a piece has been cared for.
candidate_elements.reason: It adds a visual identity that C3 lacks and ties the two tiers together. It stays optional because some clients prefer invisible repair, and it is a detail, not the platform, so the kintsugi-borrowing risk is limited.

candidate_elements.element: Provenance record for each remade garment, holding the owner's story and the atelier's work
candidate_elements.purpose: Records the garment's new chapter, supports authenticity and keeps the owner's story attached to the piece for later reuse or inheritance.
candidate_elements.reason: It fits the story-led core and costs little at couture scale. Only a light version is included, for remade pieces and opted-in owners, to avoid the heavy infrastructure and privacy issues that led to C1's rejection.

candidate_elements.element: Atelier skills content: short films and a few workshops where petites mains show basic care and repair
candidate_elements.purpose: Humanises the artisans, supplies supporting content throughout the lead-up and shows people how to extend the life of garments they own.
candidate_elements.reason: The process documentary already centres the artisans, so skills content is a natural extension. It is kept as a supporting chapter, not a standalone programme, so the mystique is protected and it does not read as charity.

candidate_elements.element: Full public lifetime provenance and resale network across all Dior products
candidate_elements.purpose: Would create a system-wide record of ownership and encourage circular resale.
candidate_elements.reason: It needs heavy infrastructure, raises privacy concerns and could push people towards resale over repair. It would dilute the focus on the anniversary and on repair.

candidate_elements.element: Open public teaching programme in many cities for repairing any brand's garments
candidate_elements.purpose: Would build a broad skills community and earn goodwill.
candidate_elements.reason: It does not drive repair of Dior's own pieces, scales poorly and risks diluting exclusivity. A small amount of skills content is enough.

candidate_elements.element: Rules on eligibility: a limited number of non-Dior garments in the couture selection, Dior-only for the service tier
candidate_elements.purpose: Settles the open question about accepting other brands' garments, keeping the call for stories broad and emotionally rich while keeping the service tier operationally and commercially coherent.

candidate_elements.element: Phased timeline: call for submissions, selection, filmed remaking, then the anniversary show, with the service tier continuing afterwards
candidate_elements.purpose: Manages the limited lead time before the anniversary and builds anticipation, with content released as the work progresses.
candidate_elements.reason: The tight timing is a stated risk. Phasing turns the process into a sustained story and keeps the campaign going after the show.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a boutique repair and alteration tier, launched at the same time as the call for submissions, so couture remakes become the showcase and not the whole offer.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Couture remakes alone reach few people and could be read as elitist or greenwashing. The service tier delivers the repair and reuse behaviour the brief needs and lasts beyond the anniversary.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set eligibility rules: a limited number of non-Dior garments may be selected for couture remaking, while the service tier is Dior-only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This resolves the open question about other brands' garments, keeping the stories open and the workload and commercial logic clear.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. People submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture pieces, filmed from first cut to final fitting, and the anniversary show closes with the owners wearing them. Remade pieces carry an optional signature stitch and a record of their story. At the same moment, Dior boutiques launch a repair and alteration service for Dior pieces, so reuse is available to many, not only the few chosen. Petites mains films share care and repair know-how along the way. The message: the most radical luxury is the piece you already love.

What happens to the remade pieces after the show: do they stay with their owners, join an exhibition or archive, or inspire a future collection, and how does that shape what Dior says about reuse?
