Second, structure the experience as a simple three-part journey: reveal (the hidden inch), refit (the service), and pass on (the next owner). Third, add emotional storytelling through real owners and the atelier hands that perform each refit. Fourth, keep leather and accessories inside the idea with named equivalents, so the inch becomes a house-wide promise rather than a tailoring detail.

borrowed_elements.element: Real owners' emotional stories of beloved, lived-in pieces
borrowed_elements.why_needed: The technical detail of a seam allowance risks feeling dry. Real owners and their garments' histories supply the emotional core that makes the inch matter to people.

borrowed_elements.element: Atelier craftspeople credited by first name and shown in close-up performing the refits
borrowed_elements.why_needed: A refit promise needs visible human skill to be believable. Showing the hands behind each inch adds credibility and warmth, and it proves the service capacity exists.

borrowed_elements.element: A pre-owned route where a refitted piece passes to a new owner, framed as 'the next inch'
borrowed_elements.why_needed: The reuse side of the topic needs a concrete route for later owners. A light version of this can be built on the inch without the full business-model change and previous-owner label of a full programme.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a published construction and repairability standard, plus a small visible mark on eligible pieces, as a core part of the idea.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The main risk is a greenwashing accusation. A checkable commitment, with a defined scope, turns the inch from a story into a promise the house can be held to.

revisions_after_selection.change: Structured the campaign as a three-part journey: Reveal, Refit, Pass On.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This makes the idea easier to execute, gives each audience (first owners, later owners, new fans) a clear entry point, and makes sure both repair and reuse are covered.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed real owner stories from C1, told through garments that have changed with their owners, and left out the deliberate-damage runway concept.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It fixes the dryness concern with emotion, and it avoids the risk of seeming to romanticise damage or devalue expensive pieces.

revisions_after_selection.change: Borrowed atelier hands credited by first name from C4 as the people performing each refit, rather than as a standalone campaign.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the service credible and human without the risk of a forgettable craft-hero trope, because the hands now serve a new service and a new device.

revisions_after_selection.change: Included a light pass-on route from C3 rather than a full certified resale programme with numbered previous-owner labels.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Reuse needs a tangible route, but a full programme is a business-model decision with cannibalisation and privacy risks. A lighter route keeps the campaign feasible and leaves room to scale later.

revisions_after_selection.change: Named leather, shoe and accessory equivalents (resole, re-edge, re-strap) as part of the launch scope.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It stops the seam metaphor from being limited to tailoring and makes the inch a house-wide promise.

final_proposal.title: The Extra Inch
final_proposal.idea: Hidden inside well-made Dior couture is an inch no one sees: extra seam allowance that lets a garment be taken in, let out and re-fitted for decades. The Extra Inch makes that secret the house's promise of a long life. Dior publishes its construction standard and marks eligible pieces. Owners can book an atelier refit, and leather, shoes and bags get their own inch through resoling, re-edging and re-strapping. Films open up real garments and follow them through changing owners, with the atelier hands credited by first name. When a piece is passed on, the inch is the room the next owner gets to make it theirs. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a purchase.
follow_up_questions: Which pieces and categories can honestly carry the inch at launch, and what standard would Dior be willing to publish and be held to?
How could the inch show up as a physical unit of measure, in the boutique, on a label or in the packaging, so owners feel it rather than just read about it?
How far should the pass-on route go, from a simple gifting-and-refit service to a house-certified resale offer, without diluting exclusivity or raising privacy concerns?

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a design guardrail: the darn must be a distinct, patented-in-spirit Dior technique with a lattice geometry that is unmistakably cannage, developed by the petites mains and shown in craft film before any consumer launch.

final_proposal.title: The Cannage Darn
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into a signature. The petites mains develop a hand-stitched mending technique built on the cannage lattice, so a mend on a well-loved Bar jacket or Lady Dior becomes a mark of devotion rather than a fix for a flaw. Owners choose a visible Cannage Darn or a discreet invisible mend. Every repaired piece returns with a card recording the date and the owner's reason for keeping it. final_proposal.idea:
Every first paycheck pays for something nobody put in the job description, and it's often making things look good. The campaign reveals that hidden line on a pay stub: 'Rescuing the café menu from Comic Sans.' 'Turning the clinic's handwritten sign into something readable.' 'Making the 6pm slide deck make sense.' Drawn from many industries and first jobs, these illustrative stubs (no real pay data) let people say 'that's me' and celebrate the accidental designer as a strength, not a grievance.

Canva then turns recognition into action: a Skills Receipt that records the hidden work, and a 'make the case' template for a first review or raise. A manager version helps teams spot and back their quiet talent. New line items, roles and industries keep the format running.
follow_up_questions: Which unofficial first-job tasks would people in your own industry instantly recognise as their hidden line item?

How could managers be invited into the idea so it feels like recognising talent and not exposing extra workload?

final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying instant, and one side effect is fewer human moments at the till. The Slow Lane gives some of that time back. final_proposal.title: Fermé pour réparations
final_proposal.idea: Once a year, Dior closes its Paris flagship to new sales and hangs a sign: Fermé pour réparations, or closed for repairs. The windows and shop floor become working ateliers where the petites mains, the house's skilled artisans, mend clients' own Dior pieces in public view. Boutiques around the world follow, so the gesture moves across time zones. The day is the public face of a repair service that runs all year, with published commitments on repair times, pricing and how many pieces are mended. Anyone with a Dior piece can bring it, including one bought secondhand. The newest bag leaves the window, and the hands that make it take its place. The message is simple: at Dior, care is as couture as newness.

How would the day change if secondhand owners were welcomed as warmly as original buyers, and what might that do to how people see the house?

focus_check.core_direction: Dior marks the New Look's 80th anniversary by inverting its 1947 gesture: the couture atelier remakes garments people cannot let go of, documented from first cut to final fitting, and the show closes with the owners wearing the remade pieces, while a boutique repair and alteration service makes the same care available to everyone.

required_elements.element: Anniversary hook and inversion of 1947 (abundance answering scarcity becomes radical luxury in what already exists)
required_elements.what_it_does: Gives Dior a credible cultural reason to speak about reuse now and frames it as a continuation of the founding myth, not a sustainability concession.

required_elements.element: Open call for a garment you cannot let go of, with its story
required_elements.what_it_does: Creates participation and emotional content, and makes the garment a memory so reuse feels personal and not like a policy.

required_elements.element: Couture atelier remake documented from first cut to final fitting
required_elements.what_it_does: Shows that reuse receives the house's highest craft, so it reads as the pinnacle of luxury, and gives the campaign its ongoing content.

required_elements.element: Show finale with original owners wearing the remade pieces
required_elements.what_it_does: Provides the hero moment and an ownable closing image that carries the idea beyond fashion media.

required_elements.element: Broader boutique repair and alteration tier launched at the same moment
required_elements.what_it_does: Turns the couture showcase into a behaviour change available to ordinary owners and answers the elitism and greenwashing risk.

required_elements.element: Clear eligibility rules (limited non-Dior garments in the couture selection, Dior-only for the service tier) and a phased timeline
required_elements.what_it_does: Keeps the call credible and operable, settles the non-Dior question and makes the short lead time workable.

required_elements.element: Signature mark and provenance record on each remade piece
required_elements.what_it_does: Lets owners carry the story of the remake with the garment and makes reuse visible and collectable, so the idea lasts beyond the show.

focus_check.development_plan: Make the idea more concrete and feasible by naming a phased roadmap (open call, selection, filmed atelier chapters, show, exhibition, boutique service continuing afterwards), by defining a simple selection principle based on story rather than celebrity or value, and by making the service tier the lasting legacy of the anniversary. Sharpen the inversion into a clear campaign line of thought: the New Look was about the new, and the 80th is about what is already yours. Keep the owner, not the house, as the hero of every piece of content.

borrowed_elements.element: Signature repair mark, optional, stitched into remade and repaired pieces
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It gives the remade garments a recognisable Dior signature and gives ordinary owners in the service tier a visible, collectable sign of devotion, which supports behaviour change after the show. It stays optional for clients who prefer invisible repairs.

borrowed_elements.element: Provenance record for each remade garment, recording the owner's story and the atelier chapter
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It preserves the story of the original owner and the remake with the piece, keeps the memory central and supports authenticity, without building the full data infrastructure of a lifetime record. It is limited to remade pieces and opt-in.

borrowed_elements.element: Atelier skills content (short films and a few workshops) as supporting material
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It extends the documented remakes into practical know-how and humanises the petites mains, which helps people care for the pieces they own, while the focus stays on Dior's own repair and reuse.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a boutique repair and alteration tier, announced on the same day as the open call and continuing after the show.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Couture remakes reach few people and risk feeling elitist or like greenwashing. A broad service makes the behaviour change real and gives the campaign a lasting outcome.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set eligibility rules: a limited number of non-Dior garments can enter the couture selection, while the service tier is for Dior pieces only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It resolves the open question on non-Dior garments, keeps the story open and generous for the hero content, and keeps the service commercially and operationally manageable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an optional signature mark (from C4) on remade and repaired pieces.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes the work visible and ownable, and encourages ordinary owners to repair, while respecting those who want invisible repairs.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light, opt-in provenance record (from C1) limited to remade pieces, without naming owners publicly unless they agree.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It keeps the garment's memory attached to it and avoids the heavy infrastructure and privacy issues that led to rejecting C1 as the lead.

revisions_after_selection.change: Phased the campaign: open call and selection first, filmed atelier chapters in the run-up, the show as culmination, then exhibition and service continuing.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The anniversary leaves limited lead time, and phasing builds anticipation and content while keeping the show achievable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Chose selection by story and emotional weight, not by celebrity or garment value, and included atelier skills films as supporting content (from C2).
revisions_after_selection.reason: It protects the idea from becoming a celebrity or luxury showcase, keeps it human, and adds practical care know-how without drifting into a charity-style teaching programme.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For its 80th anniversary, Dior answers abundance with what already exists. The house invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, and the story behind it. The couture atelier remakes a selection into new pieces, filmed from first cut to final fitting. The anniversary show closes with the original owners walking in their remade garments. Each piece carries an optional Dior repair mark and a note of its story. On the same day, Dior opens a repair and alteration service in boutiques for Dior pieces, so the idea reaches beyond couture. The New Look becomes an act of renewal: the most luxurious thing you can wear is what you already love.
follow_up_questions: How could the selection of stories be made so that an everyday garment with deep meaning outweighs a famous or valuable one, and how would the public see that choice?
What would the boutique repair and alteration service need to feel as special as couture, such as ritual, speed, a named artisan or a visible mark, while staying accessible?
How can the campaign continue after the anniversary show, so that remade garments, owner stories and repair behaviour keep growing as a lasting Dior practice rather than a one-time event?

final_proposal.title: Slow Tap
final_proposal.idea: The tap saved us seconds. Slow Tap gives a few back. It is opt-in for both sides, so no one has to say they are lonely. Standard tapping stays exactly as fast as ever. candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the reunion a place to happen, supports small-business goodwill and gives merchants a reason to join without a heavy kit.

candidate_elements.reason: It risks feeling like surveillance and would undermine the opt-in, trust-led character of the idea.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Issuer integration is the main executional barrier. A pilot proves the idea before scaling.

final_proposal.title: Overdue
final_proposal.idea: Nobody dreads a catch-up as much as they dread an overdue notice, so Mastercard turns one into the other. People list the friends, relatives and old colleagues they owe time. Their issuer app, or a simple opt-in site, sends a mock notice: 'Amount due: one coffee, one catch-up. Overdue by 14 months.' When both people tap their own Mastercard at a partner local venue, the first round is rebated. Prefer a call or a walk? That settles it too, and cash is fine. Debts can be snoozed or forgiven, and 'you're owed one' lets anyone invite instead. An annual Overdue Day and shared results, with a loneliness charity partner, keep it going. The debt is paid by showing up.
follow_up_questions: What would the most affectionate and funniest overdue notice sound like for a friend you haven't spoken to in five years, versus a parent you speak to weekly?
How could the idea reach people who feel they have no one to put on their list, without making them feel singled out?
Where else could the language of finance (interest, statements, refunds, credit) be turned into a warm human ritual, and would it extend Overdue or become a separate idea?

final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into his hems for luck. Lucky Thread revives that superstition as a ritual of repair. reader_needs.point: The insight: the most emotional work document is also the ugliest and least understood.
reader_needs.why: The whole idea rests on this tension, so if the reader misses it the campaign looks like a template giveaway.

reader_needs.point: What Canva actually makes and who uses it.
reader_needs.why: A B2B reader needs to see a concrete product and a clear action for employers, not just a feeling.

reader_needs.point: What Canva will not do: no payroll data, no tax or financial advice.
reader_needs.why: This is the biggest risk, and stating the boundary early builds trust in the idea.

reader_needs.point: How the idea can grow beyond one document.
reader_needs.why: The reader must see a platform that can carry other work documents, not a one-off activation.

terms_to_explain.explanation: The document that shows what an employee earned, what was taken out and what they actually received for a pay period. It is also called a payslip.
Amounts taken from gross pay before the employee receives it, such as tax, pension and insurance contributions.
A template designed so an employer's payroll or HR system can feed its data in, while Canva handles only the look and wording of the page.

tone_choices.choice: Warm and plain, with short sentences and little jargon.
tone_choices.reason: The idea is about making things clear, so the proposal itself should be clear.

tone_choices.choice: Lead with the human moment before the product.
tone_choices.reason: It keeps the idea from sounding dry and mirrors how the campaign itself would be told.

tone_choices.choice: Confident but careful about claims, with the limits stated directly.
tone_choices.reason: Canva is not a financial adviser, and a clear boundary makes the idea more credible, not less.

Show how it is told: before/after stub and a first-time earner's story.
Set the boundaries and the growth path to other work documents.

final_proposal.title: First Stub: the pay stub, finally readable
final_proposal.idea: Your first pay stub is one of the most emotional documents you will ever receive, and one of the hardest to read. Canva redesigns it as a clear, human one-page story: hours become a visual timeline, deductions get plain-language labels, and there is space for a personal note from the team. It launches as a free template kit that employers and HR teams customise and send with a new hire's first pay. Canva handles only layout and wording. Figures and accuracy stay with the employer's payroll provider, and there is no tax or financial advice. Film and social show a before/after stub and one first-time earner finally understanding what they earned. The approach can then extend to offer letters, benefits sheets and reviews.

Which HR or payroll partners could help the template carry real data, and what would make them want to join?
After the pay stub, which work document would people most want made human next, and what would change if it were?

final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into hems for luck. Lucky Thread revives that ritual. final_proposal.title: The Second Signature
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into status. Owners can keep the creases, scuffs and patina of a life lived, and have the atelier mend only what is needed, either invisibly or with a visible, hand-stitched mark signed by the named petite main who made it. That mend is the piece's second signature: proof of a life lived and of the maison's own hand, which no resale platform or outside repairer can offer. The campaign launches on three icons, the Bar jacket, Saddle bag and Lady Dior, via a waiting list, and shoots real owners and their mended pieces with the reverence of a runway look, using macro photography of thread and needle. final_proposal.title: The Cannage Darn
final_proposal.idea: Dior turns repair into a signature. Its petites mains develop a hand-stitched mend based on the cannage lattice. Owners choose a visible mend, a collectible mark of a well-loved piece, or an invisible one. Each piece returns with a dated card recording why it was kept, which stays with the piece as its history passes to later owners. The campaign celebrates the most-worn Dior pieces, scuffs and all, starting with the Bar jacket and Lady Dior. It launches in appointment-only repair salons for Dior pieces, with published turnaround times, and grows through film, runway and an archive of owners' stories. Repair stops being a fix for a flaw and becomes proof of a piece worth keeping.

How could the campaign celebrate well-worn pieces so that it honours long, careful ownership and never reads as encouraging damage?
How should the mend and its card pass between owners over time, and what would that history be worth to a piece's story and desirability?

candidate_elements.purpose: Turns a solo moment into an invitation and adds a shareable mechanic.
candidate_elements.reason: It adds a promotional offer that would overshadow the central point about time. It also risks implying that eating alone is a problem, which contradicts the stigma-free strength of the Slow Lane.

candidate_elements.element: Sending a friend a small 'first round is on me' gift with a message.
candidate_elements.purpose: Lowers the awkwardness and cost of reconnecting with a friend.
candidate_elements.reason: It enters a crowded digital gifting space, only helps people who already have someone to contact, and moves the campaign from a place-based experience to a transactional product feature.

revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects the many people who are happily alone, avoids forced interaction, and keeps the idea stigma-free.

revisions_after_selection.change: Framed the campaign publicly around time, not loneliness. Loneliness is the strategic purpose but is never the label on the counter.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Nobody should have to identify as lonely to use it, and the framing 'speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't' is more inclusive and shareable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Scoped the first phase as a small, well-resourced pilot on a few streets chosen with community partners and aggregated area-level insight, with a merchant kit and local promotion.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Manages merchant willingness and the gimmick risk, and creates real proof points before scaling to a national programme.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined success through participation, merchant stories and opt-in customer feedback, and made no claim of directly reducing loneliness.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Loneliness impact is hard to measure directly, and overclaiming would damage credibility.

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying instant. The Slow Lane gives some of that time back. In a pilot on a few local streets, independent cafés, bakeries and corner shops mark one counter as a Slow Lane: a stool, no queue pressure, and someone happy to chat if you are. The terminal still completes the payment in a blink, then says 'Take your time.' Nothing is labelled as loneliness support, so anyone can use it, whether they want a word or just a sit-down. Mastercard owns the irony openly: speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't. Shops get a simple kit, local promotion and optional conversation tips from community partners. Pilot streets are chosen with those partners and aggregated area-level insight. Success is tracked through participation, merchant stories and opt-in customer feedback.

focus_check.development_plan: Make the idea sharper by giving it a single, memorable reveal moment (the opening of a seam to show the inch) and a clear campaign line of thought: the garment is designed to change with you. Make it more concrete with a named service (The Next Inch), a visible inch mark sewn into newly made and refitted pieces, and a published standard for minimum allowances. Make it more feasible by phasing: start with couture and ready-to-wear jackets, coats and dresses in selected ateliers and flagships, add leather and shoe equivalents next, then extend to reuse and handover. borrowed_elements.element: Real owners' emotional stories of beloved, lived-in pieces

borrowed_elements.element: Atelier hands performing the refits, credited by first name and shown in close-up
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It makes the service tangible and trustworthy, showing who actually delivers the promise and giving the invisible inch a human face.

borrowed_elements.element: Owner number two as a later extension of the reuse pathway
borrowed_elements.why_needed: It gives the reuse side a clear next step, so the inch continues to a second owner, without committing Dior to a full resale business model at launch.

revisions_after_selection.change: Named the service 'The Next Inch' and made it a bookable refit and repair offer with a visible inch mark (a small contrast stitch or label) on new and refitted pieces.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a published construction standard for minimum seam allowances and a commitment to match atelier capacity before launch, phased by category and city.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The longevity claim must be provable and deliverable, or it invites greenwashing accusations and disappointed clients.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined inch equivalents for leather goods, shoes and accessories (resoling, re-edging, re-strapping, re-stitching) under the same 'next inch' language.

revisions_after_selection.change: Built the campaign narrative around real owners' refit stories, filmed with the atelier hands doing the work.

final_proposal.title: The Next Inch
final_proposal.idea: Inside a well-made Dior garment hides an extra inch of seam allowance, left so the piece can be taken in, let out and refitted for decades. The campaign opens that seam and makes the inch Dior's quiet promise: this was made to change with you. It launches The Next Inch, a bookable atelier service for refits and repairs, with equivalents for shoes and leather goods, a published construction standard, and a small inch mark on new and refitted pieces. Real owners tell the story, from a wedding dress taken in to a coat let out and handed to a daughter, while atelier hands do the work on camera. Luxury stops being a purchase and becomes a long relationship, and passing a piece on becomes the next chapter.

final_proposal.idea: We made paying take a heartbeat. Some of the day's only human contact went with it. final_proposal.title: First Paid
final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: a bakery menu, a wedding invitation, a first client deck. Canva invites people to share a First Paid receipt, a card that pairs that piece of work with the date, the person who paid them, and an amount they can blur or hide. Together the receipts form a public gallery of the work that started careers, and 'Made in Canva' becomes a badge of pride. Anyone can join, from freelancers to students, and 'work' includes résumés and pitches. We seed the gallery with creators and staff before launch. The gallery also gives teams real proof of Canva in action.

focus_check.core_purpose: Loneliness is a growing problem, and Mastercard needs a meaningful way to address it for people who have drifted out of social life because inviting and accepting invitations has started to feel costly, awkward or like a burden.
focus_check.core_direction: Mastercard makes reaching out free and easy to accept: any cardholder can send a digital invitation to a coffee, meal or class, and Mastercard covers the guest's first item at a participating local merchant, so the message becomes 'It's covered. Just come.'

required_elements.element: A simple digital invitation that any cardholder can send to anyone, and a guest who can accept without needing a card or an account
required_elements.what_it_does: Puts the first move in the hands of people who already know someone, so the idea reaches isolated people through existing relationships, with no labelling of 'lonely people' and no barrier for the guest.

required_elements.element: Mastercard covering the guest's first item at participating local merchants
required_elements.what_it_does: Removes the cost barrier and the fear of being a burden, and turns Priceless from a tagline into a working mechanism.

required_elements.element: Human, person-first invitation framing and a sender-written note
required_elements.what_it_does: Keeps the idea from reading as a discount promotion. The invite is a personal gesture from one person to another, and the free item is the reassurance, not the headline.

required_elements.element: Caps, fraud controls and a phased launch in a few markets

Add an 'invite again' prompt so one coffee can become a habit. Design safeguards: per-card caps, merchant-set off-peak windows, single-use codes and a pilot in a few markets. final_proposal.title: The Covered Invite
final_proposal.idea: People don't only stop going out; they stop asking, and they stop saying yes, because they fear the cost and being a burden. The Covered Invite removes both. final_proposal.title: Owe Me One
final_proposal.idea: When you split a bill or cover a coffee, a new option appears beside 'Pay back': 'Settle in person.' Instead of sending money, you propose a date. A payments brand choosing not to finish a transaction is the provocation: time with people is the one currency that can't be sent digitally. It simply makes seeing each other the easiest way to pay.

writing_notes.intended_reader: A marketing or brand lead, possibly at Mastercard or an agency partner, who knows the brand and the Priceless platform but has not seen the earlier directions. They are busy, will skim first, and want to judge quickly whether the idea is clear, original and workable.

reader_needs.point: The human barrier: people stop inviting as well as stop attending, because of cost and fear of being a burden.
reader_needs.why: The whole idea rests on this insight, so the reader must accept it before the mechanism makes sense.

reader_needs.point: The mechanism: a cardholder sends an invitation and Mastercard covers the guest's first item at a local business.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs to picture exactly what happens, in one step, to judge whether it is simple and credible.

reader_needs.point: Why Mastercard owns it: it makes Priceless a working gesture by paying for the seat so the moment can be priceless.
reader_needs.why: Ownability is what separates this from a generic loneliness or discount campaign.

reader_needs.point: How it grows and stays safe: themed invitations, seasonal moments, merchant benefit, capped launch in a few markets, measured results.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs to see that the idea can last for years and that the main risks have been considered.

terms_to_explain.explanation: Mastercard's long-running brand platform, built on the idea that the best moments in life cannot be bought, though the everyday things around them can.
Customers visiting a shop or cafe during its quiet hours, which helps a small business earn money when it would otherwise be empty.
An invitation counts as redeemed when the guest actually turns up and uses the covered item.

tone_choices.choice: Warm, plain and personal, with no jargon and no marketing language such as 'offer' or 'promotion'.
tone_choices.reason: This keeps the idea reading as a human gesture rather than a discount, which is the main tonal risk.

tone_choices.choice: Never use the words 'lonely people' to describe the guest or sender.
tone_choices.reason: Labelling people would stigmatise them. The idea works through ordinary relationships, and the wording should show that.

tone_choices.choice: Short sentences, concrete examples and one clear claim per sentence.
tone_choices.reason: A busy reader should grasp the idea in under a minute and be able to repeat it to others.

outline: The insight: people stop inviting, not only attending.
The idea in one line: 'It's covered. Just come.'
How it works: sender, guest, local business, Mastercard covers the first item.
Why it is Mastercard's to own: Priceless becomes a working mechanism.
How it grows: themes, seasons, merchant benefit and regular-style welcomes.
How it launches and is judged: capped, phased, measured by invites sent, accepted and redeemed.

clarity_checks.check: Word limit and density
clarity_checks.how: Count the words in the idea text and cut anything that repeats a point, so it stays at or under 150.

clarity_checks.check: One-step mechanism test
clarity_checks.how: Read the how-it-works sentences as a stranger and confirm they say who sends, who receives, who pays and where it happens.

clarity_checks.check: Jargon and label scan
clarity_checks.how: Check that every specialist term is either explained or removed, and that no wording labels people as lonely or vulnerable.

clarity_checks.check: Questions are open
clarity_checks.how: Confirm each of the three questions cannot be answered yes or no and invites the reader's own ideas.

revisions_after_selection.change: The guest does not need a Mastercard or any account to accept; they receive a simple code or link to redeem.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The people who most need an easy way back into social life may not be cardholders, and a card requirement would exclude them.

revisions_after_selection.change: The invitation leads with the sender's personal message, and Mastercard's role appears only as 'It's covered'.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This reduces the risk that the idea reads as a discount promotion and keeps the focus on the relationship.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a launch plan with spending caps, fraud controls and a small number of pilot markets.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This answers the mechanics, fraud and merchant-network concerns raised earlier before they become blockers.

revisions_after_selection.change: Brought in C1's strongest elements: participating businesses can offer a regular-style welcome, and real regulars and owners supply stories.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps the warmth and small-business value of the rejected direction while the invitation remains the core mechanism.

revisions_after_selection.change: Dropped any targeting or detection of isolated people; the idea relies only on senders choosing to invite.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This avoids the stigma and privacy concerns that led to rejecting C3 and C4.

final_proposal.title: It's Covered
final_proposal.idea: People who feel disconnected often stop inviting others, worried about the cost or about being a burden. Mastercard removes both. Any cardholder can send a personal invitation to a coffee, a meal or a class, and Mastercard pays for the guest's first item at a participating local business. The guest needs no Mastercard. The invitation says one thing: 'It's covered. Just come.' Invitations can be themed, such as new neighbour, old friend or first one back, and timed to moments like the holidays. Small businesses gain customers in quiet hours and can add a regular-style welcome. Priceless becomes a working gesture: Mastercard pays for the seat so the moment can be priceless. It launches in a few markets with caps and fraud checks, and reports invitations sent, accepted and redeemed.
follow_up_questions: Think of someone in your own life who has stopped reaching out. What would make sending that first invitation feel easy for them?
What would make accepting an invitation as easy as sending one, for someone who is out of practice at saying yes?
Which moments in life, such as moving, retiring, becoming a parent or losing a partner, would make the most meaningful invitation themes in your market?

element_review.selected_core_idea: Once a year Dior closes its flagship and boutiques to new sales under a 'Closed for repairs' sign, and turns the shop floors and windows into public ateliers where petites mains mend clients' own Dior pieces.

candidate_elements.element: A year-round repair offer (standing atelier service, clear pricing and turnaround, booking in every boutique and online) that the annual day publicly launches and celebrates
candidate_elements.purpose: Answers the biggest concern, that a single closure day reads as a stunt. It turns the day into the public face of a lasting service and gives people a reason to act the other 364 days.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief is repair and reuse, which is a behaviour, not an event. Without a standing service the idea is only theatre. This supports the core idea and does not replace it.

candidate_elements.element: Open the day to Dior pieces bought secondhand, vintage or inherited, not only first-hand purchases
candidate_elements.purpose: Reaches resale buyers and younger people with hand-me-down pieces, the audience C1 would miss, and signals that Dior pieces have a long life across owners.
candidate_elements.reason: Reuse means pieces changing hands. Welcoming secondhand owners makes the gesture more credible and widens reach at little extra cost to the idea.

candidate_elements.element: Annual public repair report: pieces repaired, turnaround times, share of repairs done in-house, and progress on materials and supply-chain commitments
candidate_elements.purpose: Meets the hypocrisy risk head on. It lets scrutiny of supply-chain practices be answered with data and gives the platform a yearly accountability beat.
candidate_elements.reason: A luxury house closing its doors for care invites questions about the rest of its business. Transparency turns that risk into credibility.

candidate_elements.element: Pre-booked repair slots plus limited walk-in capacity, with a live view of the ateliers for people who cannot visit
candidate_elements.purpose: Manages the operational complexity and demand across many boutiques and extends the spectacle beyond the people on the street.
candidate_elements.reason: A single day with unlimited demand would produce queues and disappointment. Booking keeps the experience premium and keeps the workload realistic for the ateliers.

candidate_elements.element: An optional signature mend, such as a tone-on-tone or cannage-pattern darn, offered as a client's choice alongside fully invisible repair
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives mended pieces a recognisable Dior detail for editorial and street-style content, and gives clients a way to wear their repair proudly.
candidate_elements.reason: It works only as an option. Invisible repair stays the default for clients who want it, so the mark is never a stigma. Only genuine wear is repaired, which avoids encouraging deliberate damage. It supports the core idea without becoming the idea.

candidate_elements.element: A story card attached to each mended piece, recording its history and repair in the owner's own words
candidate_elements.purpose: Brings in the emotional richness of C4 by treating each piece as a life lived in Dior, and creates a stream of human stories for PR and social.
candidate_elements.reason: It is cheap and fits naturally into a repair interaction. It adds emotional depth without turning the day into a second event.

candidate_elements.element: Replace the website homepage with the 'Fermé pour réparations' sign and a booking link for the day
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes the closure complete and credible across channels, so the gesture is not undermined by an open online shop.
candidate_elements.reason: A closure that excludes online sales would look half-hearted. Showing the sign online costs little and amplifies the single image.

candidate_elements.element: A runway show built from clients' returned and reinterpreted pieces
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds fashion-world prestige and a big emotional finale.
candidate_elements.reason: It is episodic and expensive, and it would shift attention from repair to reinterpretation. It can be a later chapter once the platform is established.

candidate_elements.element: Lifetime alteration promises, generous seam allowances and replaceable components in a dedicated capsule
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the repair message product substance at the design stage.
candidate_elements.reason: It needs a slow, costly redesign of production and is better treated as a long-term roadmap that the platform can later point to. The core idea works with existing pieces from day one.

candidate_elements.element: Public mending workshops where petites mains teach basic repair skills to non-owners
candidate_elements.purpose: Spreads repair skills and broadens participation beyond Dior owners.
candidate_elements.reason: It would dilute the focus on Dior pieces and compete for scarce atelier time on an already demanding day. It could be explored in later editions.

final_proposal.title: Fermé pour réparations
final_proposal.idea: Once a year, Dior hangs a sign on its Avenue Montaigne flagship: 'Fermé pour réparations.' No new products are sold. The shop floor and windows become working ateliers where petites mains mend clients' own Dior pieces, bought new or secondhand, in full public view. Boutiques worldwide do the same, and the website swaps its homepage for the sign. Each repair gets a small story card, and clients choose an invisible mend or a discreet signed one. The day is the public face of a repair service open every day, and Dior publishes an annual report on pieces repaired, turnaround times and materials progress. Luxury's most valuable space goes to care instead of newness, as proof that a Dior piece is meant to be kept, mended and passed on.
follow_up_questions: What other prime luxury 'real estate' (windows, campaign slots, Fashion Week, the website) could be handed over to care instead of newness, and what would each one say about the house?
What would a repair experience look like if it felt as prestigious as buying, such as a ten-year-old bag returned with a ceremony and a record of its history?
How could the sign and the day speak to people who do not yet see themselves as Dior clients, such as someone who inherited a jacket or bought a piece secondhand?

final_proposal.title: It's Covered
final_proposal.idea: People don't only stop going out; they stop inviting, because of cost and the fear of being a burden. It's Covered lets any Mastercard cardholder send a personal digital invitation to a coffee, meal or class at a participating local merchant. Mastercard pays for the guest's first item, so the message is simply: 'It's covered. Just come.' The note can add 'no pressure, no need to reply today.' Merchants, often neighbourhood regulars' spots, greet invited guests and offer a quiet off-peak seat. After redeeming, guests can invite someone else. Invites can be themed (new neighbour, old friend, 'first one back') and timed for moments like the holidays. Caps, code redemption and a phased launch keep it fundable, and the campaign tells real invitation stories rather than offers. The seat is paid for, so the moment can be priceless.
follow_up_questions: Which invitation moments carry the most hesitation (a new neighbour, a friend you have drifted from, a colleague after a job change), and which would make the strongest first theme?
How could the invite itself be designed so that accepting feels like a gift to the sender rather than a favour owed, and what would that look or sound like?
What would success look like beyond redemptions, for example a second meeting, a standing weekly plan or a guest becoming a host, and how could that be captured without tracking private lives?

element_review.selected_core_idea: At the moment of a peer-to-peer payment between friends, offer a 'Settle in person' option that replaces the money transfer with a scheduled meetup, so a payments brand chooses time together over completing the transaction.

candidate_elements.element: Partner cafes and restaurants as 'settle-up' venues, with a small perk or a table held for the meetup (e.g. the first coffee is on the house)
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the scheduled meetup a ready place to happen and a reason to follow through. It also adds a partnership layer to the platform and uses existing Priceless relationships.
candidate_elements.reason: The main risk for C4 is that meetups never happen. A venue and a small nudge raise follow-through and give the pilot something to measure. It supports the core idea and does not change it. It stays with friends who already know each other, so none of C1's stranger-safety issues apply.

candidate_elements.element: Matching strangers or acquaintances into open seats at shared tables
candidate_elements.purpose: Would extend reach to people who have few friends to owe.
candidate_elements.reason: It brings back the safety, moderation and ownability problems that led to C1's rejection, and it dilutes the simple 'you owe a friend' truth. The idea works because the bond already exists.

candidate_elements.element: Optional personal name or nickname shown on the 'Owe Me One' invite (e.g. 'Sam owes you one')
candidate_elements.purpose: Makes the invitation feel personal and ties it to the True Name platform.
candidate_elements.reason: The invite is already between two people who know each other, so a name adds little. It also invites a platform-integration debate that distracts from the core mechanic.

candidate_elements.element: Mastercard 'tap' sound reworked as a short chime that confirms the shared date, replacing the usual payment confirmation
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the idea a distinctive sensory signature and links to Mastercard's sonic identity, so the 'unpaid' moment still feels like a completed transaction.
candidate_elements.reason: It is a low-cost, ownable cue that makes the counter-intuitive moment feel rewarding and not like a failed payment. It supports the idea and is easy to demo in film and social.

candidate_elements.element: Graceful fallback: if the meetup is not confirmed or does not happen within a set window, a gentle prompt offers to reschedule or to send the money as usual
candidate_elements.purpose: Protects the user experience and the friend's trust, and answers the concern that meetups may not happen.
candidate_elements.reason: Without it the idea is a gimmick that can leave someone unpaid. With it the idea is credible and safe to pilot. Debts are never lost.

candidate_elements.element: Pilot with a P2P or banking app partner in one city, plus a public 'meetups kept' counter
candidate_elements.purpose: Supplies the real product and proof of usage that C4 needs to avoid reading as a stunt, and gives the campaign a living metric to report on.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief's main concern is credibility. A small live pilot with real results is more persuasive than a concept film, and the counter gives PR and social a continuing story.

candidate_elements.element: Social and content series 'Who do you owe one?', where people publicly name a friend they owe time to and are prompted to book it
candidate_elements.purpose: Extends the idea beyond the app so people who never use the product can take part, and builds cultural reach.
candidate_elements.reason: It carries the insight to a wide audience and keeps the stigma-free positioning, since anyone can take part. It is the awareness layer that points back to the pilot.

candidate_elements.element: Retailer 'Slow Lanes' staffed for conversation at checkout
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds a physical in-store expression of the human-connection theme.
candidate_elements.reason: It depends on retailer operations, has limited scale, and moves the human moment from friends to merchants. It would dilute the single, sharp idea.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a fallback so an unconfirmed or missed meetup prompts a reschedule or a normal payment after a set window.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Meetups may not happen, and nobody should be left unpaid. The fallback protects trust in a financial product.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added partner cafes and restaurants as optional settle-up venues with a small perk, borrowed from C1's venue approach but limited to existing friends.
revisions_after_selection.reason: A ready place and a small nudge raise follow-through and strengthen the partnership layer, without the safety issues of matching strangers.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a distinctive confirmation chime based on Mastercard's sonic 'tap', borrowed from C2.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It makes choosing time over money feel like a completed, rewarding moment and gives the idea an ownable sensory cue.

revisions_after_selection.change: Framed the first phase as a one-city pilot with a P2P partner and a public 'meetups kept' counter.
revisions_after_selection.reason: It gives the idea a real product and proof of usage, so it does not read as a gimmick.

revisions_after_selection.change: Kept the positioning free of any mention of loneliness in the user experience; the topic appears only in campaign storytelling and results.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Not labelling anyone as lonely is the idea's main strength. Keeping it out of the product keeps participation stigma-free.

final_proposal.title: Owe Me One
final_proposal.idea: When you split a bill or cover a friend's coffee, a new option appears beside 'Send': Settle in person. Instead of moving money, the app sets a shared date, and a Mastercard chime confirms it. A payments brand choosing not to complete the transaction is the provocation: time with people is the one currency that can't be sent digitally. Partner cafes hold the table and add a small perk. If the meetup slips, a gentle nudge offers to reschedule or pay as usual, so nobody is left out of pocket. Phase one is a one-city pilot with a P2P partner and a public counter of meetups kept. 'Who do you owe one?' carries the idea into social and content, inviting everyone to see a friend they've been meaning to.
follow_up_questions: What is the smallest real product moment (a button, a prompt, a partner app) that would let us test 'Settle in person' within a few months, and who would be the right partner?
Beyond meetups kept, what would count as proof that this reduces isolation without ever asking people to say they are lonely?
How could the 'owe one' idea grow into a recurring cultural ritual, such as a yearly day for settling up in person, that other brands and communities want to join?

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying faster. Now it says: not everything should be. In partner grocers, pharmacies and markets, one checkout lane is set aside to take its time. The sign reads 'This lane takes its time.' It is open to everyone, whether you want a chat, a calm moment or just aren't in a hurry. Cashiers opt in as Slow Lane hosts, with recognition and protected time. On the terminal, an optional Slow Tap swaps the efficient beep for a warmer sonic pause. A pilot in off-peak hours tests the business case with merchants and a wellbeing partner, and the results are published. If it works, it grows into Slow Hour and Slow Day. For many people living alone, the checkout is the only conversation of the day. This lane makes it a good one.

Where else in everyday life, such as pharmacies, post offices, ticket counters or bus fares, is speed taking out the human moment, and what would a 'slow' version look like there?

reader_needs.point: Why the buyer is the employer or HR team, and what action we ask of them.
reader_needs.why: This is what makes it a B2B idea and not a consumer sentiment piece.

reader_needs.point: The boundaries: presentation and plain-language labels only, no tax or financial advice, with payroll accuracy staying with the employer's provider.
reader_needs.why: The reader must see that the main legal and credibility risk has been handled in the design.

terms_to_explain.explanation: The document that comes with a payment and shows hours worked, gross pay, deductions and net pay. It is also called a payslip or pay statement, depending on the country.
Amounts taken from gross pay before the worker receives it, such as tax, pension and insurance contributions.
A template built so that payroll or HR software can feed data into it, with fields and spacing that anticipate real payroll output.

tone_choices.choice: Lead with the human moment, then move to the product and the business case.
tone_choices.reason: The emotion is the strongest asset of the idea, and leading with it avoids the 'dry document' risk.

tone_choices.choice: Use plain, concrete language and avoid agency jargon.
tone_choices.reason: The idea is about clarity, so the proposal should demonstrate it.

tone_choices.choice: State the limits of the idea directly, in a calm and confident voice.
tone_choices.reason: Naming the no-advice boundary early builds trust and shows the idea is thought through.

outline: The insight: the first pay stub is the most emotional and least understood document of a working life.
The idea: Canva redesigns it as a clear one-page story with a timeline, plain labels and a personal note.
How it works: a free template kit that employers customise and send with the first pay.
Why employers act: a better onboarding moment that puts Canva inside HR workflows.
How it shows up: before/after storytelling led by a real first-time earner.
Limits and growth: no financial advice, payroll data stays with the provider, and the approach extends to other work documents.

clarity_checks.check: Is the insight clear in the first two sentences?
clarity_checks.how: Read only the opening lines and confirm a newcomer could repeat the tension between feeling and format.

clarity_checks.check: Is every term understandable without outside knowledge?
clarity_checks.how: Replace or define payroll and design jargon in plain words on first use.

clarity_checks.check: Is the employer action concrete?
clarity_checks.how: Confirm the text names who does what, namely HR customises the template and sends it with the first pay.

clarity_checks.check: Does the text stay within 150 words and make no financial claims?
clarity_checks.how: Count the words and scan for any wording that sounds like tax or money guidance.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the idea from 'a prettier pay stub' to a 'first pay moment' kit, with the personal note as the lead feature rather than an add-on.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This protects against the risk of feeling dry and keeps the emotional core the client asked for.

revisions_after_selection.change: Set a firm boundary: Canva designs the presentation and plain-language labels only, with a visible disclaimer that figures and accuracy belong to the employer's payroll provider.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Canva is not qualified to give tax or financial guidance, and this removes the biggest credibility and legal risk.

revisions_after_selection.change: Made the employer or HR team the explicit target of the call to action, with payroll and HR platform partnerships as a second route to adoption.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The campaign depends on employers using the template, and partnerships reduce that dependency.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned freelancer first-invoice stories (from C1) and the stub-style thank-you card (from C3) as optional supporting content rather than parts of the core idea.
revisions_after_selection.reason: This keeps the core focused while still using the best elements of the rejected directions.

final_proposal.title: First Stub: the pay stub, made human
final_proposal.idea: Your first pay stub is one of the most emotional documents of your working life, and one of the ugliest. Nobody explains it. Canva redesigns it as a clear one-page story: hours become a visual timeline, deductions get plain-language labels, and there is space for a personal note from the team. It ships as a free template kit that HR teams customise and send with a new hire's first pay. Canva handles the design only. It gives no tax or financial advice, and the numbers stay with the employer's payroll provider. The campaign leads with a real first-time earner finally understanding what they earned, shown in a simple before/after. It can then grow to offer letters, benefits sheets and onboarding packs.
follow_up_questions: Which moment in a new hire's first week would your own team most like to make feel human?
What other work document do people receive but never really understand, and what would it look like if it were clear?
Which HR, payroll or onboarding partners could carry the template to employers who would never search for it?

final_proposal.title: First Paid
final_proposal.idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it. First Paid invites people to publish a receipt for the work that started their career: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. Each receipt shows the design, the date and who paid, with the amount optional and blurred by default. It starts as a gallery seeded with creators and well-known names, and 'first thing I made for someone' keeps it open to people whose first pay was not for design. Teams can help new hires make a receipt for their first project, a First Invoice pack helps freelancers get started, and receipts later feed city-by-city stories. 'Made in Canva' stops being a watermark and becomes a badge that marks where a career began.
follow_up_questions: What is the most surprising or moving first paid piece of work you have seen, and what would it take to make a stranger stop scrolling on it?
How should the receipt look so it feels like a keepsake worth printing or framing and not another social template?
Which real workplaces, schools or communities could run First Paid as a ritual, and what would make a manager want to do it every time someone new joins?

revisions_after_selection.change: Broadened the campaign's story engine from heirlooms and inheritance to moments of change in the present (a new job, a changed body, a move, a new city), with inherited pieces as one chapter among many.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The main risk is a nostalgic, heirloom-only tone that feels old and misses younger audiences. Anchoring stories in the life someone is living now keeps the idea current and widens its appeal.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a light authentication and eligibility step for secondhand pieces, with the Second Fitting label issued only after the atelier has verified the item.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Servicing pieces of unknown origin raises brand-control and counterfeit risks. A verification step protects quality and exclusivity while keeping the idea open to secondhand owners.

revisions_after_selection.change: Planned a phased launch: a limited atelier capacity with published turnaround times and pricing, then expansion by city as capacity grows. Launch communications would feature only real clients and real atelier work.
revisions_after_selection.reason: The promise breaks if the atelier cannot deliver, and staged stories would make the service feel purely commercial. Scoping capacity first and using real transformations protects credibility.

revisions_after_selection.change: Folded C3's visible-mend motifs (star, muguet, bee) in as an optional finishing choice, rather than a headline feature. Also folded in C2's record of a piece's life as a simple client ledger entry, without any resale marketplace.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Both elements add personalization and continuity at low cost, but neither is strong enough to carry the idea. Keeping them as options avoids the derivative and transactional readings that counted against C3 and C2.

final_proposal.title: Second Fitting
final_proposal.idea: Dior built its name on the first fitting, the moment a garment is made for one body. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be re-fitted for the life its owner is living now: a Bar jacket let out for a new body, a mother's coat recut for her daughter, a Lady Dior re-edged. Each finished piece receives a dated, signed Second Fitting label and an entry in a client ledger. The campaign is told through real transformations and the named petites mains who perform them, so keeping a Dior piece becomes the ultimate status act. Launch begins in a few cities with published timelines, and secondhand pieces are verified before they are accepted.
follow_up_questions: What is the smallest, most honest version of Second Fitting that the atelier could deliver well at launch, and how would you communicate its limits as a mark of exclusivity rather than a shortcoming?
Which present-tense moments of change (a promotion, a new city, a changed body, a farewell) could make this feel relevant to a 25-year-old as much as to a lifelong client?
How might the signed label and client ledger become something people want to show and talk about without turning the idea into a resale or tracking system?

reader_needs.why: If the reader cannot retell the idea in one breath, they cannot judge it or carry it forward.

reader_needs.point: Why this idea suits Dior and this moment: it inverts the 1947 gesture, with abundance then and what already exists now.
reader_needs.why: The cultural hook and the link to the founding myth are what make it Dior's idea and not a generic sustainability campaign.

reader_needs.point: A broader repair and alteration service in boutiques launches at the same moment as the couture remakes.
reader_needs.why: This answers the elitism and greenwashing risk and shows the idea changes everyday behaviour as well as making a spectacle.

reader_needs.point: How the campaign unfolds in phases: submissions, selection, documented remaking, the show and then continuing services.
reader_needs.why: The reader needs to see it is feasible within the limited lead time and can grow into a platform.

terms_to_explain.explanation: Christian Dior's first collection in 1947, with its soft shoulders, cinched waist and very full skirts, which answered postwar austerity with abundance.

The everyday boutique offer of repair and alteration for Dior pieces, open to many more people than the couture selection.

tone_choices.reason: A senior reader judges ideas faster when they are described as things that happen, not as concepts.

final_proposal.title: The New Look, Again
final_proposal.idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture, filmed from first cut to final fitting. The anniversary show closes with the owners wearing their remade pieces. On the same day, Dior's boutiques launch a repair and alteration service for everyday Dior pieces, so the idea reaches beyond the few. Each remade piece carries an optional discreet repair mark and a provenance record. Reuse stops being a concession and becomes the highest form of luxury.

final_proposal.title: The First Thing You Made
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck wasn't payment for your time. It was payment for the first thing you made: the shop flyer, the chalkboard menu, the rota, the slide the boss needed by Monday. The campaign invites people to rebuild that first piece of work, from memory if needed, and place it beside the paycheck it earned, then share the story behind both. Canva makes the remake easy and turns it into a keepsake. Employers extend it into 'First Thing You Make Here', marking a new hire's first deliverable and first payday together. Every career starts with something you made.

final_proposal.idea: Owe Me One turns the smallest debt between friends into a reason to meet. writing_notes.intended_reader: A Mastercard marketing or brand lead, or an agency colleague, who knows the brand and its Priceless platform but has not followed the worksheet. They are deciding whether the idea is worth developing, so they need it to be clear, short and credible.

reader_needs.point: The idea in one picture: a marked counter with a stool, no queue pressure and a friendly chat, plus a terminal that says 'Take your time'.
reader_needs.why: If the reader can picture it in a few seconds, they can judge it and retell it to others.

reader_needs.point: The truth behind it: Mastercard made payment fast, and one side effect is fewer human moments at the till.
reader_needs.why: This is what makes the idea honest and ownable rather than a generic kindness campaign.

reader_needs.point: Nobody has to be lonely to use it, and chatting is always optional.
reader_needs.why: This explains how the idea avoids stigma and why it can reach isolated people without singling them out.

reader_needs.point: How it starts and grows: a small pilot with a simple merchant kit and community partners, then a wider small-business programme.
reader_needs.why: It shows the idea is realistic and that the main risk, merchant participation, has an answer.

terms_to_explain.explanation: A marked counter or till in a participating local shop or café, with a stool, no pressure to hurry and staff happy to chat if the customer wants to.
Paying so quickly and easily, by tap or phone, that there is almost no pause or interaction at the till.
A simple pack for shop owners with signage, terminal screen copy, a stool and short guidance for staff, so joining takes little effort.

tone_choices.choice: Warm and plain, with no clinical language about loneliness or isolation.
tone_choices.reason: The idea works because it is for everyone, so the wording should not label or pity anyone.

tone_choices.choice: Candid about Mastercard's own role in making payment fast.
tone_choices.reason: Owning the side effect makes the stance credible and heads off the charge of hypocrisy.

tone_choices.choice: Short, concrete sentences that describe what happens rather than abstract claims about connection.
tone_choices.reason: Concrete detail makes the idea easy to picture and keeps it within the word limit.

outline: Open with the product truth: payment got fast, and human moments at the till got fewer.
State the idea: the Slow Lane, a marked counter that gives time back.
Describe what the customer sees and hears, including the terminal line 'Take your time'.
Explain why it is open to everyone and why chatting is optional.
Show how it starts and scales: pilot streets, merchant kit, community partners, wider programme.
Close with the brand stance and three open questions for further thinking.

clarity_checks.how: Make sure the text names the stool, the unhurried counter, the friendly staff and the terminal message in plain words.

clarity_checks.check: Is every term explained or avoided?

revisions_after_selection.change: Wrote Mastercard's role in frictionless payment into the core message instead of leaving it implied.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Owning the side effect directly answers the hypocrisy risk and makes the stance honest and distinctive.

revisions_after_selection.change: Reframed the launch as a small pilot on a few streets with a simple merchant kit, rather than a broad rollout from day one.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Real merchant willingness and staff buy-in are the biggest risk, and a resourced pilot lets them be tested before scaling.

final_proposal.title: The Slow Lane
final_proposal.idea: Mastercard made paying take a fraction of a second. One side effect is fewer human moments at the till. The Slow Lane gives some of that time back. Participating local shops and cafés mark one counter with a stool, no queue pressure and a staff member happy to chat if you are. The terminal reads 'Take your time' while the payment still completes instantly. Nobody has to say they're lonely: the lane is open to everyone, and talking is always optional. The campaign owns Mastercard's part in the speed-up openly: speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't. Start with a pilot on a few streets, with a simple merchant kit, signage and local community partners, then grow into a wider small-business programme.
follow_up_questions: Where else in everyday life has convenience quietly removed a human moment, and how could a brand give it back?
What would make a shopkeeper or café worker want to host a Slow Lane rather than feel obliged to?
How could we tell that an unplanned conversation happened, without labelling anyone as lonely?

final_proposal.title: The First Thing You Made
final_proposal.idea: Your first paycheck was payment for the first thing you made. Maybe it was a flyer for the corner shop, a chip-shop menu, a shift rota or a slide for your boss. We invite people to bring that creation back and pair it with the pay it earned. If they didn't keep it, they can rebuild it from memory in Canva, and handwritten signs and price lists count too. The result is a keepsake of where working life began. Employers can join by inviting new hires to make a 'first thing I made here' in week one, turning onboarding into a small celebration. Every career starts with something you made.
follow_up_questions: Which first creation, such as a hand-painted sign or a rota, would make you stop scrolling, and what would that tell you about who to feature first?
What small welcome ritual could a manager run in a new hire's first week that feels like a celebration rather than a task?
How might the first creation be passed on to the next new starter without turning the campaign into advice-giving?

focus_check.core_direction: Turn Christian Dior's lily of the valley superstition into a repair ritual in which every piece mended or restyled by the atelier receives a hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining that cannot be bought, only earned by keeping the piece alive, with the mending artisan credited by name.

required_elements.what_it_does: Protects the quality of the embroidery and the repair, so the ritual is never diluted or overpromised.

required_elements.element: A light lineage record that logs each repair and sprig
required_elements.what_it_does: Lets resale, authentication and the archive recognise the mark, so mended pieces hold or gain value and keeping a piece is rewarded beyond the sentimental.

final_proposal.title: Lucky Thread
final_proposal.idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into his hems for luck. Lucky Thread turns that superstition into Dior's repair ritual. When a piece comes back to the atelier to be mended or restyled, an artisan finishes it with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining and signs the repair with their name. final_proposal.idea: Pay Together is a small gift of money that only works when two people are in the same place. You send a friend, neighbour or colleague a virtual Mastercard worth a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles. It unlocks only when both of you tap phones at a local independent venue. element_review.selected_core_idea: At the moment of a peer-to-peer payment between friends, Mastercard offers 'Settle in person', which replaces the money transfer with a shared, scheduled meetup, so that a small debt becomes a reason to see each other.

candidate_elements.element: Partner cafes and restaurants as 'settling places' that host or reward settled-in-person meetups (e.g., the first coffee on the house, or a reserved 'Owe Me One' table)
candidate_elements.purpose: Gives the meetup a physical home and makes the idea easy to see and experience. It supports small businesses and gives the campaign a credible place for PR and for measuring real meetups.
candidate_elements.reason: The selection already named cafe and restaurant partnerships as a platform leg, and C2's neighbourhood-commerce appeal fits it. It supports the core idea without depending on retailer operations changes, because the venue is a host and not a redesigned checkout.

candidate_elements.element: Open Seat: an option to invite a third person (a neighbour, a colleague, a friend of a friend) to the settled meetup
candidate_elements.purpose: Widens the circle beyond a pair and could help people who have fewer close ties.
candidate_elements.reason: It brings back stranger-matching, safety and moderation concerns, and dilutes the clear two-person bond that makes the core idea simple. It can be considered later as a phase-two extension.

candidate_elements.element: Chosen-name display in the invitation and calendar prompt, using the name the friend has chosen (True Name)
candidate_elements.purpose: Adds personal warmth and reuses a proven Mastercard asset.
candidate_elements.reason: In a P2P flow between friends, names are already known, so the benefit is small. It would also add complexity and raise privacy questions without making the core idea stronger.

candidate_elements.element: Graceful fallback: if the meetup is not confirmed or not held within a set window, a gentle nudge is sent and the user can convert to a normal payment in one tap, with no penalty or guilt
candidate_elements.purpose: Protects the user experience and the trust of a financial brand, and addresses the main concern that meetups may not happen.
candidate_elements.reason: The brief's concerns call for it, and the idea cannot work as a payments feature without a safe path back to a completed transaction.

candidate_elements.element: A 'meetups kept' tally shown as a shared counter (not a debt balance) and used as the campaign's proof of real usage, with anonymised aggregate data for PR
candidate_elements.purpose: Shows the idea works, avoids the gimmick risk, and gives the campaign a living number to report and build on.
candidate_elements.reason: It answers the gimmick concern directly. It is kept aggregate and opt-in to avoid surveillance or privacy worries.

candidate_elements.element: A pilot with a P2P partner or a working prototype and a limited launch (one city, one P2P app or Mastercard-supported wallet) before any wider rollout
candidate_elements.purpose: Meets the need for a product or credible prototype and keeps cost and risk manageable.
candidate_elements.reason: The main concern for this direction is delivery. A small, real pilot makes the idea believable and gives content and proof.

candidate_elements.element: A new default for the 'I'll get you back' phrase, built into social content under the prompt 'Who do you owe one?', with creators and the public tagging the friend they owe
candidate_elements.purpose: Turns a product feature into a cultural conversation and extends reach beyond pilot users.
candidate_elements.reason: It supports the platform idea and lets people take part without having the feature, widening reach while staying true to the core.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added partner cafes and restaurants as hosts of settled-in-person meetups, with a small reward for the pair, such as a first drink offered.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Gives the idea a physical, visible home, supports small businesses and creates a clear, measurable partnership leg, without relying on the checkout changes that weakened C2.

revisions_after_selection.change: Built in a one-tap fallback to a normal payment, with a gentle reminder and no guilt-based messaging.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Meetups may not happen. The fallback protects user trust and the payment promise and removes the biggest practical objection.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a shared 'meetups kept' counter, opt-in and aggregate, as the campaign's proof of usage.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Real, reported meetups prevent the idea from reading as a gimmick and give PR and content a growing number.

revisions_after_selection.change: Defined the launch as a small pilot in one market with a P2P partner or prototype, not a global product release.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Addresses the need for a product or pilot partner and keeps the first step credible, affordable and testable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Left out Open Seat (C1) and True Name display (C3) from the core, and kept Open Seat as a possible later extension only.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Both add risk (stranger safety, privacy) or little value in a friend-to-friend flow, and would blur the simple two-person idea.

final_proposal.title: Owe Me One
final_proposal.idea: When you split a bill or cover a friend's coffee, a new option appears beside 'Send': 'Settle in person'. Instead of moving money, the app sets a shared date to meet, and a partner cafe or restaurant can host it with a small treat. If the plans fall through, one tap converts it to a normal payment, no guilt. A payments brand choosing not to complete a transaction is the provocation: time with people is the one currency that can't be sent digitally. Launch as a one-city pilot with a P2P partner, share an opt-in count of 'meetups kept', and run the social question 'Who do you owe one?' so everyone can take part, without anyone being labelled lonely.
follow_up_questions: What is the smallest real pilot (one city, one P2P partner, one venue group) that would prove people actually meet, and what number of kept meetups would make it a story?

How could the idea reach people who have few friends to owe, without labelling them or reintroducing stranger-matching, for example through a 'thank you' owed to a neighbour, a colleague or a family member?
If 'Owe Me One' became a recurring cultural ritual (a day, a phrase, a tradition), what would make it belong to Mastercard and not just to any payments app?
